passages.h: PFA Academy Foundations: how to read a medicine
passages.x: Most harm done to animals with medicine in India is not done by the wrong drug. It is done by the right drug in the wrong strength, by the wrong route, for the wrong species, or from a bottle that spent a summer in a car. This module gives you the vocabulary to avoid all four.

passages.h: 1.1 What is actually in the box: brand, molecule and strength Every medicine has one true name, the generic or molecule name, and any number of brand names. The
passages.x: Meloxicam is meloxicam whether the carton says Melonex, Metacam or a chemist's own brand. The dangerous variable is not the brand but the strength : how many milligrams of the molecule sit in one tablet or one millilitre. Human meloxicam tablets are 7.5 mg and 15 mg. The veterinary oral suspension for dogs is 1.5 mg per mL, and the injection is usually 5 mg per mL. A 5 kg dog on a correct 0.1 mg per kg dose needs 0.5 mg. One human 7.5 mg tablet is fifteen times that.

passages.h: 1.1 What is actually in the box: brand, molecule and strength Every medicine has one true name, the generic or molecule name, and any number of brand names. The
passages.x: The same is true of the antibiotic amoxicillin-clavulanate, which comes as 375 mg and 625 mg human tablets, veterinary 250 mg and 500 mg tablets, and paediatric syrups of several strengths. Reading "give one tablet" without reading which tablet is how overdoses happen.

passages.h: 1.3 Reading a prescription line, and the abbreviations vets use A complete prescription line answers seven questions: which animal, what weight, which molecule,
passages.x: An example, as it might be written for a 12 kg community dog with tick fever: Doxycycline 100 mg tab, 1/2 tab PO BID x 28 days, with food. Read it as: doxycycline, 100 mg tablets, half a tablet, by mouth, twice a day, for twenty-eight days, given with food. Half of 100 mg is 50 mg, which for 12 kg is about 4.2 mg per kg twice daily, inside the published range of 5 mg per kg twice a day or 10 mg per kg once a day. The arithmetic is checkable, which is the point of writing it out.

passages.h: 1.6 Who may prescribe, who may give, and what a layperson may do The Indian Veterinary Council Act 1984 reserves the practice of veterinary medicine to register
passages.x: Section 57 of the Act makes it an offence for anyone else to practise veterinary medicine, and the definition of veterinary medicine is wide: modern scientific veterinary medicine in all its branches, including surgery and obstetrics. Choosing a drug, a dose and a course for an animal is practice. Following a prescription is not.

10 kg × 0.1 mg/kg = 1 mg, which is 0.67 mL of the 1.5 mg/mL suspension. A 7.5 mg tablet is 7.5 times the dose, and half of it is still nearly four times. Same molecule, different strength, different dose.

passages.h: 2.1 Pain and inflammation: NSAIDs, and the four that India has banned for animals Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) block the enzymes that make pro
passages.x: The veterinary NSAIDs a vet in India reaches for are meloxicam Rx (dogs, cats with great care, cattle, buffalo), carprofen and firocoxib (dogs), tolfenamic acid (dogs, cats, cattle), flunixin (cattle, horses) and phenylbutazone (horses). All are given with food, with the animal drinking normally, and never alongside a steroid or a second NSAID. The warning signs of trouble are vomiting, black or tarry stool, refusing food, and drinking or urinating more than before; any of these means the drug stops and the vet is told the same day.

passages.h: 2.1 Pain and inflammation: NSAIDs, and the four that India has banned for animals Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) block the enzymes that make pro
passages.x: India has removed four NSAIDs from veterinary use because of what they did to vultures, which died of kidney failure after eating carcasses of treated cattle: diclofenac (withdrawn from veterinary use in 2006, with the formal prohibition under Section 26A of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act gazetted in 2008), ketoprofen and aceclofenac (notification of 31 July 2023), and nimesulide (gazetted in January 2025). Aceclofenac turns into diclofenac inside a cow. Meloxicam is the vulture-safe alternative and is what the Vulture Recovery Plan recommended in place of diclofenac.

passages.h: 2.2 Steroids: the most useful and most misused injection in India Corticosteroids such as prednisolone and dexamethasone Rx suppress inflammation and the immune
passages.x: At anti-inflammatory doses (prednisolone around 0.5 to 1 mg per kg a day in dogs) they relieve itch and swelling; at immunosuppressive doses (2 to 4 mg per kg a day) they switch off the immune response, which is intended in immune-mediated anaemia and dangerous in an infection. Predictable effects are thirst, hunger, more urine, panting and a thin coat; longer courses bring muscle loss, a pot belly, skin infections and, in cats, diabetes. Steroids and NSAIDs together ulcerate the gut; this pair is the single most common dangerous combination in animal medicine.

passages.h: 2.2 Steroids: the most useful and most misused injection in India Corticosteroids such as prednisolone and dexamethasone Rx suppress inflammation and the immune
passages.x: Two Indian specifics. Dexamethasone in the last trimester of a cow or buffalo's pregnancy can bring on calving and abortion. And the "one dexa injection" given to any animal that looks unwell, without a diagnosis, is how a treatable infection is masked until it is untreatable.

passages.h: 2.3 Antiparasitics: dewormers, tick and flea products, and the two that must never touch a cat Parasites are the commonest treatable disease in Indian animals,
passages.x: Worms. Pyrantel (roundworm, hookworm), praziquantel (tapeworm, including the Echinococcus that causes hydatid disease in people) and fenbendazole (a three-day course; also for Giardia ) are the usual dog and cat dewormers OTC in India ; combination tablets are dosed by weight band on the label. Puppies are dewormed from two to three weeks of age and every two weeks until weaning, then monthly to six months. Livestock get albendazole, fenbendazole, levamisole, ivermectin, and closantel or triclabendazole for liver fluke in flood-prone districts; the ICAR goat calendar recommends deworming before and after the monsoon and at least fifteen days before vaccinating.

passages.h: 2.3 Antiparasitics: dewormers, tick and flea products, and the two that must never touch a cat Parasites are the commonest treatable disease in Indian animals,
passages.x: Ticks and fleas. Fipronil spot-ons (dogs and cats), imidacloprid, selamectin, and the newer isoxazoline chews (fluralaner, sarolaner, afoxolaner) Rx , which also treat sarcoptic and demodectic mange in dogs and have made ivermectin injections for mange largely unnecessary. Deltamethrin collars and cattle pour-ons, and amitraz dips, are for dogs and livestock only.

passages.h: 2.4 Antihistamines: what they can and cannot do about an itch Antihistamines block one messenger of allergy. They help with an acute reaction, a wasp sting, a v
passages.x: The ones on Indian prescriptions are chlorpheniramine, cetirizine and diphenhydramine by mouth, and pheniramine (widely sold as Avil) by injection, which vets use for acute allergic reactions and sometimes to blunt reactions to antivenom. Sedation is the main side effect; in cats chlorpheniramine can cause excitement instead. Human "cold and flu" tablets that combine an antihistamine with a decongestant (pseudoephedrine, phenylephrine) are dangerous to dogs and cats and must not be used.

passages.h: 2.6 Fluids: reading dehydration, and what may be given by mouth Dehydration kills more sick animals in India than the diseases that caused it. It is also the on
passages.x: Lift the skin over the shoulder blades and let go. In a hydrated animal it snaps back at once; in a dehydrated one it stands or sinks slowly (the "skin tent"). Press a finger on the gum until it whitens and release: colour should return in under two seconds. Gums that are dry and tacky, eyes that look sunken, and a heart racing faster than the ranges in Lesson 7.2 all point the same way.

passages.h: 2.6 Fluids: reading dehydration, and what may be given by mouth Dehydration kills more sick animals in India than the diseases that caused it. It is also the on
passages.x: What a caregiver may do: offer water, or an oral rehydration solution if a vet has advised it, to an animal that is conscious, can swallow and is not vomiting. Small amounts often, never forced by syringe into a mouth that cannot swallow. What belongs to the vet: fluids under the skin (common for a dehydrated dog or cat that is still drinking a little) and fluids into a vein, where the rate is calculated for the animal's weight and a wrong rate drowns a small animal from the inside.

passages.h: 2.7 Hormones: oxytocin in the dairy, and the contraceptive injection that causes cancer Two hormone products are misused on Indian animals at scale. One is a cr
passages.x: Oxytocin Rx is a Schedule H hormone with real uses in labour and in retained placenta, under a vet. Injected into a cow or buffalo to force milk let-down it causes pain, does not make more milk, damages the reproductive tract, and is an offence: Section 12 of the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act 1960 punishes anyone who performs "phooka" or "doom dev" or any operation, including the injection of any substance, to improve lactation in a way injurious to the animal, and the animal is forfeited to the government. Its retail sale has been repeatedly restricted by the Centre for exactly this reason.

passages.h: 2.7 Hormones: oxytocin in the dairy, and the contraceptive injection that causes cancer Two hormone products are misused on Indian animals at scale. One is a cr
passages.x: Hormonal contraceptive injections for dogs, usually medroxyprogesterone acetate, stop heat cycles for a season. They also cause pyometra (a pus-filled uterus that kills), mammary tumours and diabetes. Sterilisation, which the Animal Birth Control Rules 2023 make the lawful way to manage community dogs, removes the uterus and the risk with it. There is no safe "injection instead of surgery".

passages.h: 2.8 The six conditions behind most sick street dogs, and what treating each involves A colony caregiver will meet the same six diseases over and over. None of t
passages.x: A 14 kg community dog in October: off food for three days, a nosebleed, small purple spots on the gums. The vet finds a platelet count of 22,000 and starts doxycycline 100 mg, one and a half tablets once a day (about 10 mg per kg) for 28 days, with food, and a tick product.

passages.h: 2.8 The six conditions behind most sick street dogs, and what treating each involves A colony caregiver will meet the same six diseases over and over. None of t
passages.x: By day ten the dog is eating and bright. The temptation is to stop. The published course is 28 days because a shorter one lets Ehrlichia persist and relapse, often as the chronic form with bone-marrow failure. The tablet is given with food and a little water because doxycycline burns the gullet if it lodges.

Diclofenac (2006), ketoprofen and aceclofenac (2023) and nimesulide (2025) are prohibited for animal use under Section 26A of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act because their residues in carcasses kill vultures. Meloxicam is the recommended alternative.
Corticosteroids and NSAIDs both remove the protection of the stomach lining. Given together they cause bleeding ulcers; this is the commonest dangerous drug combination in animals.
Cats cannot metabolise permethrin. A dog spot-on applied to a cat, or licked off a treated dog, is a life-threatening emergency. Use a product licensed for cats.

Antibiotics are the medicines most often given to Indian animals without a diagnosis, and the ones whose misuse reaches furthest: into the milk on a doorstep, into the soil of a colony, and into the hospital ward where a resistant bacterium eventually turns up in a person. This module is about using them so that they keep working.
State what antibiotics act on and the three common conditions they do not treat.
Recognise the antibiotic classes on an Indian veterinary prescription and each one's signature risk.
Apply the five rules of a course and explain a withdrawal period to a farmer.

passages.h: 3.1 What antibiotics do, and the three things they do not Antibiotics kill bacteria or stop them multiplying. They have no effect on viruses, on fungi or on par
passages.x: Parvovirus, distemper, kennel cough (mostly viral), ringworm (a fungus) and worms are not cured by an antibiotic. Sometimes a vet still prescribes one alongside a viral disease, as in parvovirus, where bacteria cross the damaged gut wall and the antibiotic prevents sepsis. That is a vet's judgement about a specific risk, not a reason to buy amoxicillin for every vomiting puppy.

passages.h: 3.1 What antibiotics do, and the three things they do not Antibiotics kill bacteria or stop them multiplying. They have no effect on viruses, on fungi or on par
passages.x: Bactericidal drugs (penicillins, cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, metronidazole) kill; bacteriostatic ones (tetracyclines, macrolides, sulfonamides) hold the bacteria still while the immune system finishes them. The distinction matters in an animal whose immune system is not working, and it is one reason the same infection is treated differently in a healthy adult and a starving puppy.

passages.h: 3.2 The classes on an Indian veterinary prescription, and each one's signature risk Eight classes account for almost every antibiotic a vet in India prescribes.
passages.x: Colistin, a last-resort human antibiotic, is banned in India for food-producing animals, poultry, aquaculture and feed supplements since 19 July 2019. It has no place in a dairy or a poultry shed.

passages.h: 3.3 The five rules of a course Right diagnosis, right drug, right dose, right interval, right duration. Miss one and the course fails or breeds resistance; miss
passages.x: Diagnosis first. An antibiotic is chosen for a bacterium, not for a symptom. "Fever" is not a diagnosis.

passages.h: 3.3 The five rules of a course Right diagnosis, right drug, right dose, right interval, right duration. Miss one and the course fails or breeds resistance; miss
passages.x: Drug fitted to the bacterium and the site. Skin, urine, gut, bone and brain each admit different drugs. The vet's choice of a "weaker" older drug is usually stewardship, not stinginess.

passages.h: 3.3 The five rules of a course Right diagnosis, right drug, right dose, right interval, right duration. Miss one and the course fails or breeds resistance; miss
passages.x: Dose by weight. Under-dosing is the classic resistance-breeder: enough drug to select survivors, not enough to kill them. The tablet made for a 30 kg dog is not "a bit strong" for a 6 kg one; it is five times the dose.

passages.h: 3.3 The five rules of a course Right diagnosis, right drug, right dose, right interval, right duration. Miss one and the course fails or breeds resistance; miss
passages.x: Interval matters. Twice a day means every twelve hours. A drug given at 8 am and 2 pm and then nothing till the next morning spends half its time below the level that works.

passages.h: 3.3 The five rules of a course Right diagnosis, right drug, right dose, right interval, right duration. Miss one and the course fails or breeds resistance; miss
passages.x: Duration as prescribed. The published course length is the shortest one shown to clear the infection. Stopping when the animal looks better leaves the hardiest bacteria alive.

passages.h: 3.4 Culture and sensitivity: what the test is, and when it is not a luxury A culture grows the bacteria from a swab, urine or pus; a sensitivity test shows whic
passages.x: It is not needed for a first, uncomplicated skin or wound infection. It is needed, and is cheaper than another failed course, when an infection comes back, when it has not improved after a proper course, when it is deep (bone, prostate, kidney, an old maggot wound), when the animal is very sick, or when a reserve antibiotic is being considered. The sample must be taken before the first dose, or the result is a list of what the antibiotic did not kill.

passages.h: 3.5 Resistance and the law: Schedule H1, the colistin ban, and residue limits India adopted a National Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance in 2017 and has s
passages.x: The World Health Organization ranks fluoroquinolones, third-generation cephalosporins, macrolides, colistin and glycopeptides as critically important for human medicine. When a vet chooses amoxicillin over enrofloxacin for a wound, that ranking is why.

passages.h: 3.6 Cattle, buffalo and goats: withdrawal periods, mastitis tubes, and the milk you must not sell Every antibiotic given to a milking animal appears in her milk
passages.x: Typical Indian dairy antibiotics are oxytetracycline, penicillin-streptomycin, enrofloxacin, ceftriaxone, and intramammary tubes for mastitis (a syringe of antibiotic pushed into the teat canal after the teat end is cleaned). Each carries a milk withdrawal, usually two to five days after the last dose, and a longer meat withdrawal. The label is specific to the product; a vet writes the discard date on the treatment record.

passages.h: 3.7 Antiseptics are not antibiotics: what to put on a wound, and what never to An antiseptic kills germs on a surface. It is the right thing for a fresh wound,
passages.x: Use: clean running water first, in quantity; then povidone-iodine diluted to the colour of weak tea, or chlorhexidine at a wound-safe dilution. Both are cheap and available at every chemist. A clean, damp dressing and a trip to the vet complete the first aid. Antibiotic ointments have a small place on superficial scrapes and none on deep or maggot wounds, where they trap what needs to drain.

passages.h: 3.7 Antiseptics are not antibiotics: what to put on a wound, and what never to An antiseptic kills germs on a surface. It is the right thing for a fresh wound,
passages.x: Never use: undiluted spirit or hydrogen peroxide in a deep wound (they kill the tissue that has to heal), phenyl or Dettol on a cat (phenolic disinfectants are toxic to cats), kerosene or petrol on maggots (they burn), turmeric, neem paste, ghee, coffee powder or tobacco (they seal in bacteria, hide the wound from the vet, and, in bite wounds, the national rabies guidelines specifically warn against applying irritants such as soil, chillies, oil, lime, herbs, chalk and betel leaves, and turmeric belongs on the same list: they damage tissue and give a false sense of treatment).

Vomiting and diarrhoea in an unvaccinated puppy is parvovirus until proved otherwise. Antibiotics do not act on viruses; the vet may still use one to prevent sepsis, at a dose for this puppy, alongside the fluids that actually save it.
Enrofloxacin is retinotoxic in cats at higher doses. This is a species-specific ceiling that does not apply to dogs, which is exactly why doses do not transfer between species.
The withdrawal period counts from the last dose, not the first. Milk sold inside it carries antibiotic residues above the FSSAI limits and into whoever drinks it.

Vaccination is the cheapest medicine in this Academy and the one most often done incompletely. A puppy given one shot is not "vaccinated"; a cow given FMD vaccine once a year is not covered; a rabies dose kept warm in a bag is water. The schedules below are the Indian ones, with the international guideline they rest on.
Explain why puppies and kittens need a series and not a shot, using maternal antibodies.
Read the Indian schedules for dogs, cats, cattle, buffalo, goats and sheep.
Run a vaccination day that does not waste the vaccine, and list the reasons vaccines fail.

passages.h: 4.1 How a vaccine works, and why "one shot" is a myth A vaccine shows the immune system a harmless version or piece of a germ so that it builds antibodies and m
passages.x: Live attenuated (modified live) vaccines contain a weakened germ that multiplies a little; they give strong, long immunity from fewer doses but are avoided in pregnant and in very sick animals. Killed (inactivated) vaccines cannot multiply, so they carry an adjuvant to provoke the immune system and need a primary course of two doses and regular boosters. Rabies vaccines for animals in India are killed vaccines.

passages.h: 4.1 How a vaccine works, and why "one shot" is a myth A vaccine shows the immune system a harmless version or piece of a germ so that it builds antibodies and m
passages.x: The reason a puppy needs three or four doses is its mother. Antibodies in the first milk (colostrum) protect a puppy for weeks, and while they last they also neutralise a vaccine before the puppy's own immune system can respond. The level and the fade-out date differ from litter to litter and from puppy to puppy, so a series given every two to four weeks until sixteen weeks of age or later is the only way to be sure one dose lands after the maternal antibodies have gone. A single early dose gives no reliable protection at all.

passages.h: 4.1 How a vaccine works, and why "one shot" is a myth A vaccine shows the immune system a harmless version or piece of a germ so that it builds antibodies and m
passages.x: Core vaccines protect against diseases that every animal of that species should be protected from because they are severe, widespread and often fatal. Non-core vaccines are given on the basis of local risk. In India rabies is core for dogs and cats because the disease is endemic.

passages.h: 4.2 Dogs: the schedule an Indian vet follows Core for dogs everywhere: distemper (CDV), adenovirus (CAV, which covers infectious hepatitis) and parvovirus (CPV)
passages.x: A titre test for CDV, CAV and CPV from twenty weeks of age can confirm the series worked; a positive result means the dog needs no core booster for three years. Rabies protection is not confirmed by a routine test in practice, which is why records matter so much when a vaccinated dog bites someone.

passages.h: 4.4 Community dogs: the ABC Rules, mass vaccination, and what a caregiver contributes The Animal Birth Control Rules 2023 make sterilisation and anti-rabies vac
passages.x: The World Health Organization's figure is that vaccinating about 70 per cent of the dogs in an area, repeated yearly, interrupts transmission. India has committed to eliminating dog-mediated human rabies by 2030 under a national action plan, and mass dog vaccination is the mechanism. Under the Rules a dog that has been through the programme is ear-notched and returned; the notch is the visible record.

passages.h: 4.4 Community dogs: the ABC Rules, mass vaccination, and what a caregiver contributes The Animal Birth Control Rules 2023 make sterilisation and anti-rabies vac
passages.x: What a caregiver does that no programme can do alone:

passages.h: 4.5 Cattle and buffalo: the NDDB schedule and the national programme Foot and mouth disease and brucellosis are vaccinated free of charge under the National Ani
passages.x: Under NADCP every vaccinated animal carries a twelve-digit ear tag and its record sits on the national livestock portal. Keep the tag legible; it is the animal's vaccination card.

passages.h: 4.6 Goats and sheep: the ICAR calendar The Central Institute for Research on Goats publishes an annual health calendar. Its first line is worth the rest: kids a
passages.x: The calendar adds two rules that apply to every species: deworm at least fifteen days before vaccinating, so the immune system is not busy with worms, and dip or spray for ticks before and after winter. Screening breeding animals for brucellosis, which passes to people, is the other habit worth keeping alongside it.
Vaccinate a healthy animal: eating, normal temperature, no diarrhoea, no recent heavy stress such as a long transport.
Deworm first; the goat calendar says fifteen days before.
Check the vial: within date, kept at 2 °C to 8 °C, reconstituted only when the animal is in front of you.
Stay twenty to thirty minutes afterwards. Swelling of the face, hives, vomiting or collapse is anaphylaxis and the vet has adrenaline for it.
Write it down: date, vaccine, batch number, who gave it. Expect a small lump and a quiet day; these pass.
Vaccinate an animal with a fever, in the middle of parvovirus, or on high-dose steroids; the vaccine will not take.
Give live vaccines to a pregnant animal unless the label allows it.
Mix vaccines in one syringe unless they are sold to be mixed.
Split one dose between two small animals. The dose is the dose whatever the weight.
Vaccinate from a vial that has been warm, cloudy or opened for more than the label allows.

passages.h: 4.9 Why vaccines fail, and how to tell that one did A vaccinated animal that gets the disease is almost never proof that the vaccine was bad. It is usually proo
passages.x: Maternal antibody was still present at the last dose: the series stopped too early, or a puppy was given one shot and called done.

passages.h: 4.9 Why vaccines fail, and how to tell that one did A vaccinated animal that gets the disease is almost never proof that the vaccine was bad. It is usually proo
passages.x: The cold chain broke , somewhere between the factory and the syringe.

passages.h: 4.9 Why vaccines fail, and how to tell that one did A vaccinated animal that gets the disease is almost never proof that the vaccine was bad. It is usually proo
passages.x: The interval was wrong doses too close together do not add up, and a second dose of a killed vaccine given months late is a first dose again.

passages.x: For distemper, adenovirus and parvovirus, a serology (titre) test from twenty weeks of age shows whether a puppy responded; WSAVA supports it as an alternative to an extra dose. For rabies, the practical proof is the record, which is why the national guidelines treat a bite from a "vaccinated" dog without documentation as a bite from an unvaccinated one.
Maternal antibodies vary between puppies and fade at different ages. Only a series ending at 16 weeks or later guarantees that one dose falls after they are gone.
Brucellosis control under NADCP is a single dose for female bovine calves aged 4 to 8 months. Adults and males are not vaccinated, and the disease is a serious zoonosis.
The ICAR-CIRG calendar asks for deworming at least fifteen days before vaccination for the best response. A heavy worm burden weakens the answer to any vaccine.

India's snakebite season is its monsoon, and dogs, cattle and goats are bitten in the same fields and yards as people. The same vial of antivenom treats all of them. The lessons here are about what is in that vial, how its dose is decided, and the ten minutes of first aid that decide whether the antivenom arrives in time.
Name the Big Four and say what Indian polyvalent antivenom does and does not neutralise.
Explain why antivenom dose follows venom, not body weight, and why it must be given by a vet.
Give correct snakebite first aid and refuse the five traditional measures that harm.

passages.h: 5.1 The Big Four, and what is in an Indian vial of antivenom Indian polyvalent anti-snake venom serum is raised in horses against the venoms of the four snakes
passages.x: The standard is written on every vial: one millilitre of reconstituted serum neutralises 0.6 mg of cobra venom, 0.45 mg of krait venom, 0.6 mg of Russell's viper venom and 0.45 mg of saw-scaled viper venom. A vial holds 10 mL. It is made in the public and private sector, among others by the Central Research Institute at Kasauli, Haffkine, Bharat Serums, VINS and Premium Serums, and it is the same product whether the patient is a child or a bullock.

passages.h: 5.1 The Big Four, and what is in an Indian vial of antivenom Indian polyvalent anti-snake venom serum is raised in horses against the venoms of the four snakes
passages.x: What it does not cover: the king cobra, the hump-nosed pit viper of the Western Ghats and other pit vipers, sea snakes, and other regional species. Venom also varies by region within a species, which is why a Russell's viper bite in one State can respond less well than in another. When the snake is known not to be one of the four, antivenom is a risk without a benefit.

passages.h: 5.2 How antivenom works, and why the dose follows the venom and not the animal Antivenom is a purified immunoglobulin fragment that binds venom molecules so tha
passages.x: A large viper can inject the same quantity into a 4 kg puppy as into a 60 kg man, and the puppy, with less blood to dilute it, needs at least as much antivenom. The vet judges the starting dose from the species of snake, the speed of the signs and the bedside clotting test, gives it slowly into a vein, and repeats it if bleeding, swelling or weakness keep advancing. There is no correct dose per kilogram of dog, which is why "one vial for a small animal" is not a rule.

passages.h: 5.2 How antivenom works, and why the dose follows the venom and not the animal Antivenom is a purified immunoglobulin fragment that binds venom molecules so tha
passages.x: Because the serum comes from horses, a minority of patients react to it, from hives to full anaphylaxis, and serum sickness can follow a week later. The vet has adrenaline drawn up before the drip starts; a skin test does not predict who will react. Reaction is a reason for the vet to be ready, not a reason to withhold antivenom from an envenomed animal.

passages.x: A 10 kg dachshund in Karnataka was brought to a veterinary college hospital with a swollen face, fang marks on the right cheek and blood-tinged fluid oozing from the bite, after a Russell's viper bite. The only abnormal blood value was a low platelet count. It was treated with polyvalent antivenom into a vein, intravenous saline, and supporting drugs for five days, and recovered fully.

passages.x: The lesson in the report is the order of events: the owner recognised the bite, carried the dog to a hospital that stocked antivenom, and the antivenom went in before the coagulopathy became bleeding.

Move the animal away from the snake without chasing or handling the snake; note its colour and pattern, or photograph it from a distance if that costs no time. Snakes are protected under the Wild Life (Protection) Act 1972; do not kill it.
Keep the animal as still as possible and carry it. A dog that walks pumps venom through its lymphatics faster.
Take off the collar; a face or neck bite swells within minutes.
Note the time of the bite and go straight to the nearest vet or veterinary hospital that stocks antivenom. Telephone ahead so the vial is out of the fridge.
If the animal stops breathing and you know how, support its breathing on the way. Krait and cobra kill by paralysing the breathing muscles, and antivenom reverses it.
Tie a tourniquet or a tight cord above the bite. It causes gangrene and does not stop viper venom.
Cut the bite or try to suck venom out. Suction removes almost none and the cut bleeds in an animal that may soon be unable to clot.
Apply ice, cold water, hot packs or electric shock. Ice worsens tissue death.
Apply herbs, "snake stones", lime, kerosene or any paste, or give alcohol or a home remedy by mouth.
Wait to see whether symptoms develop. By the time they are obvious, the antivenom has more to do and less time.

passages.h: 5.5 Where the antivenom is, and how to keep it Antivenom is stocked at government primary and community health centres and district hospitals for people, and at
passages.x: The freeze-dried form keeps for five years in a cool, dark place and is reconstituted with 10 mL of the diluent supplied; the liquid form keeps for two years at 2 °C to 8 °C and must never freeze. Both are protected from light and heat, which rules out the rescue-vehicle glovebox. Reconstituted serum is used at once.

passages.h: 5.6 Cattle, buffalo, goats and horses: the bite you cannot see Large animals are bitten on the muzzle and lower legs while grazing at dusk, and their thick hide
passages.x: The particular danger for horses and cattle is a swollen muzzle that closes the nostrils. Horses breathe only through the nose; a vet may need to place a tube to keep the airway open. Treatment is the same antivenom into a vein, fluids, and management of the bleeding and the tissue damage that follows a viper bite.
Antivenom neutralises venom molecule for molecule. A snake injects the same amount regardless of the victim, and a small animal has less blood to dilute it. The vet titrates the dose to the response.
Tourniquets, cutting, suction, ice and waiting all worsen the outcome. Stillness and speed to antivenom are the only measures that help.

An immunoglobulin is an antibody given ready-made. It works within hours and fades within weeks, which makes it the right tool for the day of a rabies bite, a snakebite, a deep wound in a horse, or a newborn's first meal, and the wrong tool for anything long-term. This module also covers the one immunoglobulin a caregiver will personally receive.
Distinguish passive from active immunity and say when each is used.
Describe rabies post-exposure prophylaxis in India well enough to insist on it for yourself.
Explain colostrum, tetanus antitoxin and maternal antibody in one sentence each.

passages.h: 6.1 Passive and active immunity: hours versus years A vaccine teaches the body to make its own antibodies: slow to start, long to last. An immunoglobulin lends
passages.x: After a serious bite, rabies immunoglobulin infiltrated into the wound neutralises virus on day zero, while the vaccine given the same day takes about a fortnight to raise the person's own antibodies to the protective level of 0.5 IU per mL. The immunoglobulin covers the gap. Given too late, or in too large a dose, it can blunt the vaccine's response, which is why the national guidelines fix its window and its maximum.

passages.h: 6.1 Passive and active immunity: hours versus years A vaccine teaches the body to make its own antibodies: slow to start, long to last. An immunoglobulin lends
passages.x: Sources of borrowed antibody: horses (equine rabies immunoglobulin, antivenom, tetanus antitoxin), pooled human plasma (human rabies immunoglobulin), laboratory-made monoclonal antibodies, and the mother, through colostrum.

passages.h: 6.2 Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis for the person who was bitten: the whole protocol In India every bite by a warm-blooded animal is treated as a possible rab
passages.x: Step one, wound washing. Soap or detergent and running water for ten to fifteen minutes, then an antiseptic such as povidone-iodine or alcohol. This alone removes much of the virus. Do not touch the wound with bare hands, do not apply soil, chillies, oil, lime, herbs, chalk or betel leaves (the guidelines' own list), nor turmeric or salt, and do not get it stitched if that can be avoided; if it must be sutured, the immunoglobulin goes in first and the stitches wait a few hours.

passages.h: 6.2 Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis for the person who was bitten: the whole protocol In India every bite by a warm-blooded animal is treated as a possible rab
passages.x: Step two, the category. Category I (touching, licks on intact skin) needs no prophylaxis. Category II (nibbling of bare skin, minor scratches without bleeding) needs the vaccine. Category III (any bite that breaks the skin, scratches that bleed, licks on broken skin or on the eyes, nose or mouth, and any bite from a wild animal) needs the vaccine and rabies immunoglobulin.

passages.h: 6.2 Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis for the person who was bitten: the whole protocol In India every bite by a warm-blooded animal is treated as a possible rab
passages.x: Step three, the immunoglobulin (Category III, once, on day 0, no later than day 7 of the vaccine course). Equine RIG at 40 IU per kg (Indian ERIG is 300 IU per mL, maximum 3000 IU), or human RIG at 20 IU per kg, or a rabies monoclonal antibody, Rabishield (approved 2016, 3.33 IU per kg) or TwinRab (approved 2019, 40 IU per kg). As much as possible is infiltrated into and around every wound; the rest goes deep into muscle away from the vaccine site. Never in the same syringe or the same limb as the vaccine.

passages.h: 6.2 Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis for the person who was bitten: the whole protocol In India every bite by a warm-blooded animal is treated as a possible rab
passages.x: Step four, the vaccine. Either the intramuscular Essen schedule, one dose in the deltoid (thigh in small children, never the buttock) on days 0, 3, 7, 14 and 28, or the intradermal schedule, 0.1 mL at two sites on days 0, 3, 7 and 28, at an anti-rabies clinic that uses it. Someone previously fully vaccinated needs only two doses, on days 0 and 3, and no immunoglobulin. Tetanus toxoid and, if the wound warrants it, an antibiotic are added.

passages.h: 6.2 Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis for the person who was bitten: the whole protocol In India every bite by a warm-blooded animal is treated as a possible rab
passages.x: The dog. A dog or cat that can be observed is watched for ten days. If it stays healthy the course may be shortened by the doctor; if it sickens or dies, the course is completed and the animal's head is sent for testing through the veterinary authority. Prophylaxis is never delayed while waiting to see.

passages.h: 6.4 Tetanus antitoxin and toxoid: the horse, the wound and the fortnight Tetanus antitoxin is equine immunoglobulin against the tetanus toxin. Given to a wounde
passages.x: Horses and donkeys are by far the most susceptible domestic animals; cattle, sheep and goats less so; dogs and cats are relatively resistant and rarely need it. The classic cases are a nail in a hoof, a castration or docking done with a dirty blade, a foaling or a deep puncture. The vet gives antitoxin and the first dose of toxoid at the same visit in different sites, then the toxoid course continues (Lesson 4.7). The signs of tetanus itself, stiffness, a locked jaw, a raised tail and the third eyelid flicking across the eye at a noise, appear days to weeks after the wound, and by then treatment is long and often fails.

passages.h: 6.5 Colostrum: the immunoglobulin every newborn must drink in its first hours Calves, kids, lambs and foals are born with almost no antibodies of their own. Eve
passages.x: The rule of thumb for a calf is colostrum within the first two hours, and about ten per cent of its body weight over the first day: roughly three to four litres for a 35 kg crossbred calf, in several feeds. By twenty-four hours the gut has closed and antibodies drunk after that are digested as protein, not absorbed. A calf that missed its colostrum is the calf that dies of scours or pneumonia at three weeks. Kids and lambs are the same in miniature; the ICAR goat calendar credits colostrum with protecting kids for their first three months.

passages.h: 6.5 Colostrum: the immunoglobulin every newborn must drink in its first hours Calves, kids, lambs and foals are born with almost no antibodies of their own. Eve
passages.x: Puppies and kittens absorb antibody for their first two to three days. Orphans who missed it are the ones a vet may put on plasma or a hyperimmune serum, and who need their vaccine series started on time. Cow's milk is not a substitute for any of them; a species-appropriate replacer or, for a puppy, a puppy milk replacer, is.

passages.h: 6.6 Hyperimmune sera for parvo and distemper: what the evidence supports Indian clinics can buy hyperimmune serum or immunoglobulin products raised against cani
passages.x: The theory is sound, borrowed antibody against a virus in a puppy that has none, and the products are used by many vets in the first 48 hours of parvovirus. Controlled evidence of benefit is limited, and a puppy that gets serum and no drip still dies of dehydration. The honest position is that they may help early, alongside intensive supportive care, and that the money is better spent on the vaccine series that would have prevented the illness.

passages.h: 6.7 Maternal antibody, again: the reason for every vaccine series The same borrowed antibody that saves a puppy in its first weeks is what neutralises its early
passages.x: Maternal antibody falls by half roughly every week to ten days, but the starting level depends on the mother's own immunity and how much colostrum the animal drank. So in one litter a puppy may be open to vaccination at eight weeks and its sibling not until fourteen. The series every two to four weeks until sixteen weeks or older, and the extra dose at twenty-six weeks, exist to catch every puppy on the far side of its own fade-out. It is not over-vaccination; it is the only honest answer to an unknown date.

A bleeding bite is Category III: wound washing, rabies immunoglobulin (or a monoclonal antibody) into the wound, and the full vaccine course starting on day 0. Observation of the dog runs alongside, never instead.
Colostral antibody is absorbed whole only in the first day. A calf that misses that window has almost no immunity for months; no injection replaces it.

passages.h: PFA Academy First aid: the first hour
passages.x: First aid is what a person with no drugs can do in the hour before a vet, and it decides more outcomes than the drugs do. The rules are the same on a highway, in a cattle shed and on a kitchen floor: keep yourself safe, keep the animal breathing and warm, stop the bleeding, do nothing that hurts, and move.

passages.h: 7.2 The sixty-second check: breathing, gums, pulse, temperature, and the numbers that mean "vet now" Four measurements you can take with your hands, a watch and
passages.x: Breathing. Count chest rises for 15 seconds and multiply by four. Look at the effort: open-mouth breathing in a cat, a stretched neck, flaring nostrils and a heaving belly are distress at any rate.

passages.h: 7.2 The sixty-second check: breathing, gums, pulse, temperature, and the numbers that mean "vet now" Four measurements you can take with your hands, a watch and
passages.x: Gums. Lift the lip. Pink is normal. Pale or white means blood loss, anaemia or shock; blue means no oxygen; brick red means heatstroke or sepsis; yellow means jaundice (tick fever, liver); brown or muddy means paracetamol poisoning. Press until white and release: colour should return in under two seconds.

passages.h: 7.2 The sixty-second check: breathing, gums, pulse, temperature, and the numbers that mean "vet now" Four measurements you can take with your hands, a watch and
passages.x: Pulse. Fingers flat on the inside of the thigh where it meets the body (the femoral artery), or a hand on the chest behind the elbow. Count for 15 seconds, multiply by four.

passages.h: 7.2 The sixty-second check: breathing, gums, pulse, temperature, and the numbers that mean "vet now" Four measurements you can take with your hands, a watch and
passages.x: Temperature. A digital thermometer, lubricated, gently into the rectum for the time it takes to beep. Over 40 °C or under 37 °C in a dog or cat is an emergency.

passages.x: Ranges adapted from the Merck Veterinary Manual reference tables (Dukes' Physiology). A value outside the range is a reason to call; a value that is changing fast is a reason to move.

passages.x: Muzzle if conscious (Lesson 7.1). Do not lift by the legs, the scruff or the tail.

passages.h: 7.3 Road accidents: moving an animal that may have a broken back Most animals hit by vehicles in India die of what is not visible: internal bleeding, a ruptured
passages.x: Slide the animal onto a flat board, a car mat, a folded blanket or a sheet held taut by two people, keeping the back straight. Two hands under the chest and pelvis for a small animal, carried level.

passages.h: 7.3 Road accidents: moving an animal that may have a broken back Most animals hit by vehicles in India die of what is not visible: internal bleeding, a ruptured
passages.x: Press on any bleeding with a clean cloth; cover wounds; keep the animal warm with a blanket even in summer, because shock chills.

passages.x: Nothing by mouth. A vomiting or unconscious animal inhales it, and an animal with a belly injury may need surgery.

passages.h: 7.3 Road accidents: moving an animal that may have a broken back Most animals hit by vehicles in India die of what is not visible: internal bleeding, a ruptured
passages.x: Check the gums every few minutes on the way. Gums going pale, a belly swelling, breathing getting faster and shallower: tell the vet on the phone, because it changes what they prepare.

passages.h: 7.5 Fractures: immobilise the animal, not the leg A badly applied splint does more damage than no splint. The safe first aid for a suspected fracture is to keep
passages.x: The signs are a limb held at an angle or dangling, a bone visible or felt under the skin, swelling and severe pain on touch. Cover an open fracture with a clean damp cloth; do not push bone back or wash the wound with anything but saline. Only if the vet is hours away and the break is clearly below the elbow or knee should a padded splint (a rolled newspaper or cardboard, bandaged loosely, joint above and joint below) be considered, and only if the animal tolerates it without struggling.

passages.h: 7.6 Heatstroke: cool first, transport second Heatstroke kills by cooking organs, and every minute above 41 °C counts. The current veterinary emergency guidance
passages.x: Into shade. Water over the whole body at once: any water cooler than the dog, and for a young, healthy dog, immersion in cold water is the fastest method.

passages.h: 7.6 Heatstroke: cool first, transport second Heatstroke kills by cooking organs, and every minute above 41 °C counts. The current veterinary emergency guidance
passages.x: Air movement: a fan, an air-conditioned car, a breeze. Evaporation does the cooling.

passages.h: 7.6 Heatstroke: cool first, transport second Heatstroke kills by cooking organs, and every minute above 41 °C counts. The current veterinary emergency guidance
passages.x: Offer water to drink if the animal is conscious; do not force it.

passages.h: 7.6 Heatstroke: cool first, transport second Heatstroke kills by cooking organs, and every minute above 41 °C counts. The current veterinary emergency guidance
passages.x: Keep cooling on the way to the vet and stop active cooling when the rectal temperature reaches about 39.4 °C, to avoid overshooting into hypothermia.

passages.h: 7.6 Heatstroke: cool first, transport second Heatstroke kills by cooking organs, and every minute above 41 °C counts. The current veterinary emergency guidance
passages.x: Vet regardless of recovery: kidney and gut damage and clotting failure appear over the next day.

passages.h: 7.6 Heatstroke: cool first, transport second Heatstroke kills by cooking organs, and every minute above 41 °C counts. The current veterinary emergency guidance
passages.x: The signs are frantic panting, thick drool, brick-red gums, staggering, vomiting or diarrhoea, and collapse; a rectal temperature above 40.5 °C confirms it. The dogs that die are the ones left in cars, chained in the sun, walked at noon, and the flat-faced breeds that cannot pant well; among livestock it is animals in transport and in tin sheds.

passages.h: 7.10 Newborns and orphans: warm before you feed, and never plain cow's milk Cold kills a newborn puppy or kitten before hunger does, and feeding a cold one kill
passages.x: Warm against your body or with a wrapped hot-water bottle, over half an hour or more. A newborn's body temperature should be around 35 to 37 °C in the first week; a cold, limp puppy is not ready to feed.

passages.h: 7.10 Newborns and orphans: warm before you feed, and never plain cow's milk Cold kills a newborn puppy or kitten before hunger does, and feeding a cold one kill
passages.x: Feed a puppy or kitten milk replacer, or a formula a vet has given you, warmed to body heat, from a bottle or syringe held so the animal sucks belly-down, never on its back. Plain cow's milk causes diarrhoea and does not have the fat or protein they need.

passages.h: 7.10 Newborns and orphans: warm before you feed, and never plain cow's milk Cold kills a newborn puppy or kitten before hunger does, and feeding a cold one kill
passages.x: Every two to three hours in the first week, including nights. Small amounts; a swollen belly means too much.

passages.h: 7.10 Newborns and orphans: warm before you feed, and never plain cow's milk Cold kills a newborn puppy or kitten before hunger does, and feeding a cold one kill
passages.x: After each feed , rub the genitals and anus with warm damp cotton until the animal urinates and passes stool; the mother would lick. Without this they cannot.

passages.h: 7.10 Newborns and orphans: warm before you feed, and never plain cow's milk Cold kills a newborn puppy or kitten before hunger does, and feeding a cold one kill
passages.x: Weigh daily on a kitchen scale. Steady gain is health; a day without gain is a call to the vet.
Nitrile gloves; a gauze roll for a muzzle; a thick towel; a torch.
Clean water or saline bottles; povidone-iodine; gauze pads and a crepe bandage; blunt scissors; a tick remover or fine forceps.
A digital thermometer and lubricant; a foldable board or a strong sheet; a blanket; a cardboard box.
Soap, for your own hands and any bite you receive.
Your own rabies pre-exposure card, and the telephone numbers: the nearest vet, the night vet, the antivenom stockist, the wildlife rescuer, the local body's dog squad.
A weighing sling or luggage scale, so every animal you hand to a vet comes with a weight.
Antibiotics, painkillers and steroids "for emergencies". They need a diagnosis and a dose, and a car boot ruins them.
Vaccines and antivenom. They live in a refrigerator.
Turpentine, kerosene, phenyl, spirit, hydrogen peroxide, turmeric and any kitchen remedy.
Human cough syrups, cold tablets and paracetamol.

passages.x: Soap and running water on the wound for fifteen minutes, then povidone-iodine. Nothing from the kitchen.

passages.h: 7.14 When you are the patient: the caregiver's own bite Every rescuer is eventually bitten or scratched. The animal's welfare does not come first at that moment
passages.x: The nearest anti-rabies clinic or government hospital today for the category assessment, immunoglobulin if the skin is broken, and the first vaccine dose; a tetanus dose if yours is not current.

passages.h: 7.14 When you are the patient: the caregiver's own bite Every rescuer is eventually bitten or scratched. The animal's welfare does not come first at that moment
passages.x: Note the animal: which one, where, its vaccination record if any, and arrange for it to be watched for ten days.

passages.h: 7.14 When you are the patient: the caregiver's own bite Every rescuer is eventually bitten or scratched. The animal's welfare does not come first at that moment
passages.x: Finish the course on the dates given. The failures in the national data are almost all late starts, missed immunoglobulin and unfinished courses.
"Cool first, transport second" is the current emergency guidance. Wet towels over the body trap heat once they warm and are far less effective than water and airflow or immersion.

Anticoagulant rodenticides act on clotting factors and the signs appear two to five days later. Early vitamin K1 treatment, guided by the exact product, prevents the bleeding. Salt is never used to induce vomiting.
A chilled newborn cannot digest; feeding it first causes bloat and death. Warm slowly, then feed the right milk. Plain cow's milk causes diarrhoea in puppies and kittens.

A dose is a weight of drug for a weight of animal, converted into a number of tablets or millilitres. Every step in that chain can be checked with a calculator, and every step is where overdoses come from: a guessed body weight, a decimal point, a tablet of the wrong strength, "twice a day" given four hours apart. This module is the arithmetic, so that a caregiver can follow a prescription exactly and catch a mistake before the animal does.
Convert a mg/kg dose into tablets or millilitres for a given animal and strength, and check someone else's conversion.
Weigh or estimate the weight of a dog, a calf and a cow well enough to dose them.
Read the label ranges of the common medicines and recognise a prescription that sits outside them.

passages.h: 8.2 From mg/kg to tablets and millilitres: three worked examples and the decimal point Three steps, always the same: multiply the weight by the dose per kilogra
passages.x: A 12 kg dog, doxycycline 5 mg/kg twice a day, 100 mg tablets. 12 × 5 = 60 mg per dose. 60 ÷ 100 = 0.6 of a tablet. Half a tablet is 50 mg (4.2 mg/kg); the vet may round to half, or choose 10 mg/kg once a day, which is 120 mg, near enough one tablet. Either way the rounding is the vet's, and it stays inside the published range.

passages.h: 8.2 From mg/kg to tablets and millilitres: three worked examples and the decimal point Three steps, always the same: multiply the weight by the dose per kilogra
passages.x: A 20 kg dog, meloxicam 0.1 mg/kg once a day, oral suspension 1.5 mg/mL. 20 × 0.1 = 2 mg. 2 ÷ 1.5 = 1.33 mL, drawn up in a syringe. Misread the dose as 1 mg/kg and the answer becomes 13.3 mL, ten times the dose, and a dog with a bleeding stomach and failing kidneys. The decimal point is the most dangerous character on a prescription.

passages.h: 8.2 From mg/kg to tablets and millilitres: three worked examples and the decimal point Three steps, always the same: multiply the weight by the dose per kilogra
passages.x: A 400 kg cow, ivermectin 0.2 mg/kg under the skin, 1 per cent injection (10 mg/mL). 400 × 0.2 = 80 mg. 80 ÷ 10 = 8 mL. The label says the same thing as "1 mL per 50 kg". If the cow was guessed at 300 kg, she gets 6 mL and the worms survive; guessed at 500 kg, she gets 10 mL, which for this drug is tolerated, but the same guess with a narrow-margin drug is not.

passages.h: 8.2 From mg/kg to tablets and millilitres: three worked examples and the decimal point Three steps, always the same: multiply the weight by the dose per kilogra
passages.x: Two things that can never be measured: less than a quarter of a tablet, and less than a tenth of a millilitre in an ordinary syringe. If the arithmetic produces one of these, the strength is wrong for the animal, and the answer is a lower-strength tablet or a liquid, not a knife and a guess.

passages.h: 8.4 Check the prescription in your hand Enter what the vet wrote and what the animal weighs; this does the multiplication and division and flags an answer that
passages.x: The checker multiplies weight by the written dose and divides by the strength. It holds no dose ranges and cannot tell whether the written dose is right for the species, the age, the kidneys or the pregnancy. That is the vet's knowledge, and Lesson 8.5 shows the published ranges only so that an obviously misplaced decimal is caught.

passages.h: 8.5 Reference: label dose ranges of the common medicines, for reading a prescription These are published ranges from standard veterinary formularies, given so t

passages.h: 8.7 Why the same drug has a different dose in a different species Dose per kilogram is not a property of the drug alone. It is the drug and the animal together,

passages.h: Colistin out of the food chain, 2019
passages.x: Prohibited for food-producing animals, poultry, aquaculture and feed. A last-resort human antibiotic that Indian poultry had been eating as a growth promoter.
Sterilisation plus anti-rabies vaccination, ear-notching and return became the lawful management of community dogs, with a recognised role for caregivers.
The puppy and kitten series now ends at 16 weeks or later with an extra dose at 26 weeks; core boosters no more than every three years; leukaemia vaccine recommended for kittens and outdoor cats.
Rabishield and TwinRab give India two lab-made alternatives to horse and human rabies immunoglobulin, with fixed doses per kilogram and no serum reactions.
Emergency guidance reversed the old advice. Wet towels and "tepid water" are out; water over the whole body, airflow, and immersion for a young healthy dog are in.
