Why dogs and cats do what they do, and what helps. 75 topics in plain words, from bringing a rescued animal home to fear, aggression, soiling and old age. Each one says where in the textbook to check it.
Bringing home a rescued dog or cat, and giving it a life with enough to do. Start here.
About a quarter of dogs given up to shelters are given up for behaviour problems, often from mistaken ideas about the cause, unrealistic expectations, or harsh training.
Most animals surrendered are between 5 months and 3 years old; animals owned for a short time are the most likely to be given up.
After adoption, dogs most often show fear, anxiety, aggression, distress when alone, soiling and attention seeking; cats most often fear, hiding, aggression, soiling, urine marking and scratching.
Common medical problems after adoption include parasites, infections, and bone and joint problems; medical causes come first.
Most animals settle well, but some take several months.
Before it arrives, set up one safe, pet-proofed room with a bed, water, food, toys and (for a cat) hiding places, a climbing frame and a litter box.
Do not give it the run of the house at first. A dog goes out for a walk and a toilet break on arrival; a cat goes straight to its room.
See a vet within 7 to 10 days, then check how it is settling after a week.
For a dog, plan toilet breaks every 2 to 3 hours when it is left, for at least the first month.
Start reward-based training early; a class helps families keep their animals.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 65 to 78.
Use a crate only once the dog has learnt to be comfortable in it.
It should let the dog stand up and turn around, and not much more, or one end becomes a toilet.
A dog not yet trained to a crate can sleep in a dog-proofed area with a chew toy; it may be unsettled at first.
Teach the crate with treats and meals inside, door open, for short spells first.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 72 to 73.
Puppies, very energetic dogs, and breeds bred for work need the most.
Exercise alone is not a treatment: a tired dog is not the same as a settled one.
Food in a bowl takes away the chance to hunt and scavenge; working for food fills time and reduces problem behaviour.
Classical or reggae music in the background has been shown to increase resting and reduce barking.
Dog parks should never be used to "socialise" fearful or aggressive dogs.
Swallowed toys can block the gut: choose toys and chews suited to the dog's size.
Hide parts of the daily food in the house or garden, or in a stuffed or frozen toy.
Sniffing walks, fetch, tug, and short reward-based training sessions.
Rotate toys so they stay new; give each dog its own quiet resting place.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 81 to 93.
Cats are most active at dawn and dusk, so that is the best time to play.
Hunting is innate and does not depend on hunger.
Where several cats share too few resources, tension and fights follow.
Cats seem to prefer fine, sandy litter, and one more litter box than there are cats is the starting point (see The litter box ).
Watching birds through a window does not suit every cat; a frustrated cat may spray or redirect its aggression.
Shelves, perches and climbing frames; hiding boxes; soft resting places, warm ones for old cats.
Scratching posts near resting places and in prominent spots.
Wand toys and food puzzles; never play with hands or feet.
Safe outdoor time if possible: a harness, an enclosed balcony, a cat-proofed fence.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 94 to 114.
Check for pain and illness first. Train with rewards, never with fear.
Joint pain and dental pain are common in both dogs and cats, and cats have more joint pain than was long thought.
Sore or itchy ears can make an animal avoid being stroked, hugged or held by the collar, or snap when it is.
Gut disease, hormonal problems, infections carried by ticks, and brain disease can all show up as behaviour change.
Pain that makes moving hard can stop an animal reaching its toilet spot or litter box.
If a behaviour plan is not working, a missed medical problem is one of the first things to suspect.
Tell the vet exactly what changed and when; a short video helps.
Ask for a calm, low-stress examination; a frightened animal can be examined under sedation.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 18 to 50.
Punishment-based training and tools such as shock, prong and choke collars are linked with more fear, anxiety and aggression.
A frightened or stressed animal cannot learn, and may not even do things it knows well.
Facing an animal with what it fears all at once (flooding) can make it worse; gradual exposure paired with good things works instead.
Advice from unqualified trainers, friends and social media is a common source of problems.
Start in a quiet place with few distractions, and use a reward the animal really wants.
Keep sessions short, and stop for a break if the animal is anxious.
For aggression, look for a trainer who works force-free, alongside a vet.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 201 to 229.
The first months shape the adult. A little gentle experience now prevents a lot of trouble later.
The best age to leave the mother and litter is probably about 8 weeks, when puppies also approach new people most readily.
Gentle handling from the first days builds emotional stability; teach the puppy to enjoy being touched and briefly held, never longer than it stays calm.
All healthy puppies should start a well-run puppy class by 12 weeks (first class between 8 and 12 weeks), once vaccinated as the vet advises.
Puppies from pet shops, and some from shelters, are at greater risk of behaviour problems such as distress when alone.
The authors describe fear periods around 8 to 10 weeks and in adolescence (6 to 12 months); another textbook notes that the evidence for a fixed window is weak (Herron 2024, p. 116; Lesson 12.5 ).
Introduce a flat collar and a light leash early, with treats; never a choke or prong collar.
Teach a basket muzzle as a game early: every dog may need one if injured or in pain.
Swap, do not snatch: trade anything in the puppy's mouth for a treat, and teach Drop it and Leave it.
Play with toys, and stop before the puppy gets overexcited; never play with hands or feet, and never punish.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 119 to 128.
A rough rule: a puppy can hold on for 1 hour plus its age in months, up to 8 hours when resting.
Dogs prefer to go on soft, porous ground, where they have gone before, and away from where they eat and sleep; these preferences form early.
Punishing accidents can teach a puppy not to toilet in front of people at all.
Leftover smell draws the puppy back, so clean accidents thoroughly.
Take the puppy out often, every 20 to 60 minutes while it is awake and supervised, and whenever one activity ends and another begins.
Go on a leash, to the same spot, by the same door, and reward it the moment it finishes there.
Clean up an accident without fuss and without involving the puppy.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 129 to 138.
Kittens raised without their mother or littermates may play and pet roughly, because they never learnt bite control; early weaning has similar effects.
Sterilisation does not have to wait for sexual maturity; waiting produces many unwanted kittens.
Playful kittens may not suit homes with very young children or frail people.
New kittens should be tested for the feline viral diseases FeLV and FIV.
Keep the kitten in one quiet, furnished room for at least the first 24 hours: food, water, a litter box, resting places, hiding spots, toys.
Open the travel box and let it come out in its own time, even if that takes hours.
Visit often and briefly, and let the kitten set the pace.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 155 to 179.
Most cats prefer large boxes; size up as a kitten grows.
Scoop at least once a day, more with several cats; empty and wash with mild soap at least monthly, or weekly with non-clumping litter.
Old soiled spots from previous cats, if not properly cleaned, can attract a new one.
Pain that makes the box hard to use is a common hidden cause.
Offer a few litters side by side and let the cat choose.
Put boxes where they are easy to reach, away from food and water, with one on each floor and one more than the number of cats.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 180 to 186.
Why a dog threatens or bites, and what keeps everyone safe while it is treated.
Lack of early socialisation, early illness or pain, harsh training and punishment can all contribute to it.
Forcing a frightened dog into the situations it fears can make the fear worse rather than better.
Punishment during an aggressive episode can increase fear, and can teach the dog to stop growling before it bites.
Pain from skin, joint, gut or hormonal illness can make an aggressive response more likely.
Treatment aims to control the problem, not cure it. The outlook is better when the aggression is mild, happens in a few predictable situations and is recent.
Keep people safe first: a leash, and a basket muzzle the dog has learnt to like, around people it has threatened.
Avoid known triggers; meet them only in planned training sessions, at a level the dog can stay calm at.
Teach simple cues such as Sit and Wait with rewards, so the dog has a safe thing to do when it is worried.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 305 to 315.
Very tasty food, long-lasting chews and past hunger make food guarding more likely, and a street dog may have been hungry long before it was adopted.
Early signs are easy to miss: stiffening, hovering over the item, blocking access. Children in particular do not read them.
Punishing these low-level warnings can make the next warning stronger, or skip it.
A growl over food is within normal dog behaviour; it is a warning, not defiance.
With good management most dogs relax about people near their food over several months, though some prized items may always need to be avoided.
Let the dog eat undisturbed, behind a gate or a closed door.
Give bones and favourite chews only in a safe, gated space, especially where there are children or other dogs.
To get something back, trade it for something better or teach Drop it with rewards. Never pull it away.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 316 to 325 and 381 to 392.
Past harsh or inconsistent punishment can make the response more intense.
Illness that causes pain or irritability must be checked by a vet.
In one study of bites to children under seven, most happened indoors, during a friendly interaction with a dog the child knew.
Young children, elderly people or people with weak immunity in the home can make keeping such a dog unsafe.
Stop whatever has triggered aggression before, including petting if that is a trigger.
Announce interactions so the dog can predict them: call the dog and say what is coming, such as Walk time.
Use only reward-based training; learn the dog's body language ( Lesson 12.1 in the Academy ).
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 326 to 337.
Too little socialisation in the puppy weeks (3 to 14 weeks of age) can contribute; so can a single frightening experience with a stranger.
Dogs left to bark at passers-by, including dogs tied up outside, are at risk of becoming territorial and fearful.
In most dogs it cannot be fully eliminated, and safety measures may be needed for life.
You do not have to introduce your dog to every visitor. Keeping it away from them is an accepted treatment.
Use a leash, and a basket muzzle if needed, in public and when visitors come; if that is not safe, keep the dog in another room.
Teach calm cues with rewards in easy settings first.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 338 to 349.
Every time barking at a passer-by is followed by the person walking on, the dog learns that barking works.
A tethered dog cannot retreat, which can build both territorial aggression and fear.
Dogs are not usually cured and may always need a barrier such as a leash or gate around unfamiliar people. Do not wait for a dog to grow out of it.
Block the dog's unsupervised view of the street through gates, windows and fences.
Teach Sit, Touch and Wait with rewards, so the dog has something to do when someone comes.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 412 to 421.

passages.h: Dogs Dogs who fight at home Dogs who live together can fight, from stares and growls to real injuries. It often starts around social maturity (1 to 3 years) or
passages.x: Careful. Never put your hands between fighting dogs. People are often bitten by their own dog, by accident or redirected aggression.
Common triggers: a new pet or person, a dog falling ill or growing old, a dog coming home after time away, or a change in the family's routine.
Dogs do not share resources the way people think is fair, and imposing human ideas of fairness does not help.
If both dogs are behaviourally normal and the triggers can be controlled, the outlook is good; if either has abnormal social behaviour, it is guarded.
Learn how to separate fighting dogs without reaching between them: reaching in is how people get bitten.
Teach both dogs simple cues with rewards, and keep valued items out of shared spaces.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 359 to 369.
Too little contact with other dogs in the puppy weeks, harsh training and punishment, and being attacked on a walk all raise the risk.
Punishing a dog as it sees another dog can teach it that approaching dogs mean pain.
Many dogs improve enough to walk calmly past other dogs; some will never safely greet or live with other dogs.
Walk at quiet times and places, on a standard-length leash, never an extendable one.
Use a well-fitting collar or harness that cannot slip; never a choke, prong or shock collar.
Turn away early when you see another dog coming, and reward calm attention to you.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 370 to 380 and 393 to 403.
An aroused dog may not tell the difference between a family member and the target. Touching or pulling a dog in that state is how people get bitten.
It usually sits on top of another problem, such as fear, territorial aggression or frustration.
If the main problem is treated and triggers can be predicted and avoided, the outlook can be good.
Do not touch, hold or scold a highly aroused dog; give it space and let it settle.
Teach it to move away to a quiet place when its triggers appear.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 404 to 411.
Pain, illness and poor senses lower a dog's tolerance for frustration.
Inconsistent rules frustrate dogs: when the same behaviour is sometimes rewarded and sometimes punished, they cannot predict what works.
It usually needs long-term management, and it can grow as dogs mature socially.
Make life predictable: clear cues, rewarded consistently, by everyone in the household.
Train in short, easy steps so the dog succeeds; an overly frustrated dog cannot learn.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 422 to 435.
Fear of the car, of new places or of strangers can already have the dog anxious before the examination starts.
Even routine handling, such as being lifted onto a table, can be frightening.
Motivated caregivers can expect substantial improvement, but gentle handling has to continue for life.
Practise gentle mock examinations at home, paired with small tasty treats.
Learn the early signs of fear so you can tell the vet team ( Lesson 12.1 in the Academy ).
Ask the vet about a plan for a frightened dog before the next visit.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 436 to 450.
Pain and illness, such as arthritis, gut disease, skin disease and an underactive thyroid, must be ruled out first; some events may be seizures.
There is no consistently effective treatment.
Severe cases often stay dangerous and can get worse over time.
A full veterinary examination before anything else.
Safety measures such as muzzles and confinement are not optional with this diagnosis.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 350 to 358.
Cats would rather run than fight. When they cannot, or when play, petting or another cat tips them over, here is what is happening.

passages.h: Cats The frightened cat that hisses and swats Given the choice, a frightened cat runs. When it cannot escape, fear turns into defensive aggression. A cat behavi
passages.x: Careful. Do not pick up, hold or stroke a cat that is behaving defensively to calm it. Serious injuries happen this way.
Warning signs: backing away, fur standing up, a fast-flicking tail, ears flat against the head, wide pupils, hissing, growling and swatting.
Too little early contact with people and other animals, a new person or pet, chasing or cornering a cat, and a home with nowhere to hide all add to it.
Brief fear is normal; fear that goes on for a long time harms a cat's health and welfare.
Expect weeks to months of treatment, with small setbacks along the way.
Give the cat plenty of resources, spread out: several feeding places, high perches, low hiding places, more than one litter box.
If it must be moved, drop a large towel or blanket over it, or guide it into a room and leave it alone to calm down.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 451 to 461.

Risk factors: many cats in or around the home, the breeding season, cats reaching maturity, a new cat in the house or the neighbourhood, a move, and too few food bowls, water bowls, litter boxes and resting places.
Aggression can be passive: one cat blocking another's way to food or the litter box. It still harms the cat on the receiving end.
Putting fighting cats back together too soon makes it last longer and get worse. With time it usually improves, but this can take many months.
Cats may learn to live together peacefully without ever becoming friends.
Separate them for part of every day to keep the peace.
Give each cat its own food, water, litter box and resting place, with high walkways and hiding boxes.
Let each explore the other's room only when both are calm.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 462 to 477.
Signs before the bite: the tail starts to flick, the ears rotate, the skin twitches.
Too much stroking, little handling when young (the window for getting used to people is 2 to 9 weeks of age), anxiety, itchy skin and painful conditions such as arthritis all play a part.
Many of these cats do not like to be carried or held.
With care, serious aggression can be stopped straight away, because it depends on how the cat is touched.
Stroke briefly, and only when the cat is relaxed and asking for it.
Stop at the first warning sign; do not stroke absent-mindedly.
Notice when the cat most enjoys contact, often at mealtimes, early morning or when people come home.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 487 to 497.
Most likely in a single young cat, a kitten raised without other kittens, or one encouraged to play with hands and feet.
It is usually normal and treatable, and most cats play less roughly as they grow up.
Uninhibited, hard play aimed at people is harder to change.
Give toys that flutter, bounce and move, and play with the cat every day.
Never play with hands, feet or loose clothing.
Avoid string, wool and toys small enough to swallow; swallowed string can need surgery.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 498 to 505.
Any cat with another form of aggression can redirect it.
Once the arousal has passed, redirected aggression is unlikely. If the trigger can be controlled, the outlook is good.
Leave an aroused cat alone until it is calm; put it somewhere quiet with food, water and a litter box.
Block the view of cats outside, and do not encourage the cat to watch or meet unfamiliar cats.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 506 to 513.
Many cats in the area, the breeding season, a cat reaching maturity, a new cat at home or nearby, and a move all raise the risk.
Fights are more common at dawn and dusk, when cats are most active.
Food left outside attracts other animals.
It can be hard to treat, especially between free-roaming cats, and severe cases take months.
Keep a home cat in at dawn and dusk if it fights outside.
Think carefully before adding a new cat to a home where territorial fights have happened.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 514 to 525.

passages.h: Cats The bold cat that attacks Some cats use aggression confidently, to get something or to end contact they do not want. Its causes are not known, and it can u
passages.x: Careful. Never leave children alone with a cat that attacks this way.
Warning signs: tail flicking, flattened ears, wide pupils, a hunched head, stillness, a low growl.
Explosive, unpredictable aggression may be too dangerous for some households, depending on who lives there.
Avoid what sets it off, including approaching, stroking or lifting the cat.
Teach Come, Sit and Off with food or a clicker; do not threaten or command.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 478 to 486.
Comforting a frightened cat does not reward its fear, though it may not calm it and can put you at risk of a bite.
Punishment and scolding make fear worse.
Forcing a frightened cat through a procedure makes the next visit harder; patience and avoiding overwhelming it matter most.
Teach the cat to like its travel box and short car rides first (see Taking a cat to the vet ).
Ask the vet team for a slow, gentle visit plan for a fearful cat.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 526 to 538.

passages.h: Dogs: fear, anxiety and being alone
passages.x: Fear protects an animal; it becomes a problem when it is out of proportion, lasts, or takes over daily life.
Fear is partly inherited; long stays in a shelter, too much time in kennels or crates, and too little socialisation as a puppy add to it.
With a plan followed, improvement is usually seen within 2 to 4 weeks. Some anxieties never fully go, especially if stress continues.
Treatment can be slow and lifelong, and for a few dogs a different home suits them better.
Interrupt a worried behaviour with a light, happy sound, then ask for something easy, such as Sit or Go to your mat, and reward it.
Keep routines predictable and give the dog a quiet place of its own.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 539 to 548.
Genes, the mother's experiences before birth, early experience and later bad experiences all shape a fearful temperament. Illness can add to it.
Shy dogs, or dogs that missed socialisation, may change little even after months; some improve to near normal, some stay fearful.
Punishment makes fear worse, can trigger fear-based aggression, and hides the signs you need to see.
Work out exactly who sets the fear off (children, men, groups, people reaching) and how close they can be before it starts; stay below that.
Pair those people, at a safe distance, with things the dog loves.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 549 to 557.
Common causes: little gentle exposure to new places and things in the first months, a frightening experience, punishment, and being pushed into the fear again and again.
Loud noises, traffic, other animals, people, bad weather and construction machinery are frequent triggers outdoors.
Improvement is likely, complete recovery less so; it takes weeks to months, and long-standing fears are harder.
Avoid full exposure to the trigger while treating; a traumatic exposure undoes progress.
Include anything the dog now links to the fear, such as the leash or a phrase, in gentle training.
A dog afraid of all outdoor activity usually needs a vet's help as well, because outings cannot be avoided.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 558 to 576.
Genes, missed socialisation, bad experiences, an unpredictable home and big changes such as a move all contribute.
Chronic anxiety can show up as repetitive behaviours, urine marking or soiling indoors.
Improvement is likely; full resolution is less so, and old problems resist change.
Remove triggers where possible and give the dog a secluded, safe area.
Learn the early signs of fear, keep the day predictable, and do not punish.
Separate animals that are in conflict at home, and make sure food, water and resting places are easy to reach.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 577 to 587.
Other anxieties (especially separation distress), noise-sensitive breeds, exposure without getting used to it, living with a noise-phobic animal, and big changes all add to the risk.
Rescued dogs may be more at risk of storm phobia: they may have missed socialisation or lived through storms as strays.
Dogs can learn to link nightfall, smoke or flashes with fireworks and become anxious before any bang.
Fireworks phobia makes dogs escape and get lost. A dog's calm at its first fireworks does not mean it will stay calm.
Training with recordings may not carry over fully to real fireworks; severely phobic dogs often relapse.
Keep dogs safely contained and supervised on fireworks nights; stay home with a new dog for its first one.
Do not shut a dog in a crate it has not learnt to like: it may injure itself trying to escape.
A collar with your number, or a microchip, helps a lost dog come home. The fireworks page has more.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 588 to 623.
Genes and poor maternal care play a part. Dogs that came through shelters and rescues are reported with it more often.
Progress can be slow, with setbacks; it can take months.
Until the dog can stay calm alone, avoid leaving it alone: day care, a sitter, friends or family, or taking it along.
Keep departures and returns low-key; leave a food-stuffed toy as a distraction.
Practise short, calm absences, building up slowly, and meet its daily needs for exercise and play.
A dog that panics, injures itself or is very destructive needs a vet's help.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 624 to 640.

passages.h: Cats: fear, anxiety and being alone
passages.x: Cats hide their distress well. Hiding, overgrooming, soiling and not eating can all be fear talking.
Cats that were sociable at the shelter tend to show less fear in a new home.
Within one to two weeks most cats become more active and curious; by about the fifth week they should be comfortable in the parts of the home they can reach.
Keep the space quiet and predictable, with several hiding boxes close by.
Gently toss a treat whenever the cat comes out of hiding or explores; never pull it out.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 641 to 651.
Genes, experiences before and after birth, too little early exposure, bad experiences and punishment all play a part; illness can add to it.
Pushing a cat into what it fears, to "socialise" it, can make the fear worse.
The earlier it is treated, the better. Some cats become near normal; shy or poorly socialised cats may change little even after months.
A steady daily routine and safe spots around the home.
Teach simple cues such as Touch or Sit with treats, and reward the cat for going to its safe spot.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 652 to 670.
Genes, missed early experiences, bad experiences, an unpredictable home and big changes all contribute.
Improvement is likely, complete recovery less so.
Block views that upset the cat, separate animals in conflict, and add food and water bowls, resting places, hiding spots and litter boxes.
Keep the day predictable, and never punish an anxious cat.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 671 to 682.
Rescued cats may be more at risk of storm phobia, having missed socialisation or faced storms as strays.
Cats can learn to link nightfall, smoke and flashes with fireworks and become anxious before any bang.
Training with recordings may not carry over fully to the real thing; severely phobic cats are likely to relapse.
Some cats will still hide, pace or stay close to you despite treatment.
Supervise and safely contain cats during fireworks.
Find a food the cat loves, and keep it for training and frightening nights only.
The fireworks page has a checklist for the night itself.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 683 to 717.
Early research links it with living only indoors, having no toys, and living without other pets.
The cat is distressed, not spiteful. Punishment has no place in treatment, which can take weeks or months, with setbacks.
Regular, predictable play and contact each day.
Toys and things to do while you are out; calm departures and returns.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 718 to 730.
Soiling indoors is the commonest behaviour reason animals are given up. It is never spite, and most of it can be solved.
Most cases respond well, if the family supervises closely for several weeks or months.
Soiling from fear, anxiety or excitement takes longer to resolve, and relapses are common.
Punishing after the fact does not teach the dog anything except to fear you.
Retrain an adult dog like a puppy: supervise or confine, take it out often, reward it outdoors (see House training a puppy ).
A vet check for urinary and gut problems.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 901 to 912.
Neutering before sexual maturity may prevent marking problems, and neutering an intact male often helps a great deal.
Most dogs improve once the triggers are managed or removed.
Punishment after the event is ineffective and creates fear.
Keep a steady routine and clean marked spots thoroughly so the smell does not invite more.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 913 to 924.
Linked factors include scented litter, the cat digging less in the litter or not covering its mess, and urinary tract disease.
Punishment is unlikely to help and may make it worse.
Medical problems must be found and treated first.
Make the spots it has used unavailable or unattractive.
Offer the ideal box: try different litters and boxes side by side and let the cat choose (see The litter box ).
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 925 to 937.
New smells, new objects, new people or animals, and cats outside all trigger it; homes with several cats are more prone, but single cats spray too.
Some cats stay strongly motivated to mark despite treatment, and marking stays higher where cats in the home are fighting.
Reduce tension between cats, separating them at the times fights happen.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 938 to 950.
Mostly normal dog behaviour in the wrong place: it changes with exercise, clear rules and rewards, not punishment.
Ignoring the behaviour for a short while and then giving in teaches the dog to try harder and longer.
Most cases respond within a few weeks to a few months.
Meet daily needs for exercise, toilet trips, mental work and company.
Give attention on your terms, with a clear start and an "All done" end.
Reward a calm alternative, such as sitting, and stop rewarding the pestering.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 951 to 958.
If everyone in the home is consistent and begging never pays, it eventually stops; it can take several weeks, and often gets worse before it gets better.
No food or attention for begging, from anyone.
Reward the dog for lying on its mat during meals.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 959 to 966.
Puppies have to be taught what is theirs to chew; the chewing phase can last a long time.
Teething, from about 14 to 30 weeks of age, can increase mouthing and chewing.
Put things away and cover electrical cords.
Give safe chews, reward the dog for using them, and swap them in when it picks the wrong thing.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 967 to 974 and 1027 to 1036.
Lack of exercise, mental work, company and clear rules all contribute.
Punishing a dog for having an item teaches it to avoid you, not the item; chasing it can turn into a game, or into guarding.
Keep counters, bins and belongings out of reach.
Trade, do not chase: offer something better and teach Drop it.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 992 to 1000 and 1061 to 1070.
It is usually not harmful, unless the faeces carry parasites, viruses or toxins.
Long-standing cases may persist despite treatment.
Call the dog to you right after it toilets and reward it, so it expects food from you, not the ground.
Teach Leave it, pick up promptly, and have a vet check the gut and diet.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 975 to 981.
Punishing normal behaviour is not justified; giving the dog somewhere it may dig works better.
With more exercise and play, play digging usually settles.
Provide shade and shelter in hot weather.
Make a digging spot, bury toys there, and reward digging in it.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 982 to 991.
Most jumping improves within two weeks of consistent training.
Most excitable young dogs calm with maturity; a few have a true medical overactivity that needs a vet.
Choose a dog for its behaviour and needs, not only its looks: some breeds need far more activity.
Turn away and withdraw attention when the dog jumps; greet it when all four feet are down.
Teach Sit as the way to say hello, and use a leash to manage greetings at first.
Daily exercise and brain work are not optional.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 1001 to 1016.
It is more common in intact and male dogs, and in anxious or stressed dogs.
When attention is withdrawn it may get worse for a while before it fades.
Look away, stop touching the dog and walk away when it mounts.
Redirect it to a cue it knows and reward that.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 1017 to 1026.
Hunting and working breeds use their mouths more.
When you stop rewarding rough play it may briefly get worse before it improves.
Allow a little gentle mouthing; end play the moment teeth press hard.
Always have a toy ready to put in the puppy's mouth instead of your hand.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 1027 to 1036.
Getting up to give food or let the dog out rewards the night waking.
If too little daytime activity is the cause, giving more usually works within weeks.
More exercise, play and company in the day; a calm bedtime routine.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 1037 to 1044.
Genes, breeding for herding or hunting, and early experience of hunting all strengthen it.
Not every species can safely live together; training reduces risk but does not cure it.
Predatory behaviour that cannot be managed has a poor outlook.
Rigorous management: secure fencing, leashes, and never leaving the dog with small animals unsupervised.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 1045 to 1053.
Roaming intact dogs father unwanted litters and spread parasites and disease.
Roaming dogs are at greater risk of injury.
Secure containment and a richer life at home resolve most cases.
Mend fences and gates, and keep doors shut.
More exercise, play and company at home; sterilisation for intact dogs.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 1054 to 1060.
Sudden movements, fast sharp turns, not being able to see out, and a full stomach make motion sickness worse.
Drive smoothly and slowly; avoid winding, bumpy roads where you can.
Short, pleasant practice trips, paired with treats.
Learn which signs are fear and which are excitement.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 1071 to 1080.
A dog that is not under control on the leash is a risk to people and to itself.
Most cases improve with consistent, reward-based training.
Teach the dog what to do instead, such as walking at your side, and reward it.
A vet check if the dog refuses to walk or seems sore.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 1081 to 1089.
Barking is often rewarding in itself, so it is hard to change; most problems need several weeks of work.
Unclear rules and unmet needs for exercise, play and company feed it.
Remove or block what sets it off, such as a view of the street.
Teach a Quiet cue with rewards, and meet the dog's daily needs.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 1090 to 1100.
Scratching, climbing, night-time crying and the rest: mostly normal cat behaviour that needs a better outlet.
In homes with several cats, scratching can also be a message to the other cats.
Given time, many cats can be taught to scratch in the right place.
There are good alternatives to declawing, which the authors advise discussing before any surgery.
Put a sturdy scratching post near where the cat sleeps and where it already scratches.
Make the furniture it targets unattractive or unavailable for a while.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 1173 to 1181.
Food and food smells left on counters draw cats up there.
Cats often learn to stay off counters while you are watching, and use them when you are not.
Punishment is unlikely to work; most cats calm with age and enough play.
Give them better high places: shelves, climbing frames, a window perch.
Keep counters clear of food, and play with the cat every day.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 1125 to 1139.
Even eye contact, saying No or pushing the cat away can count as attention and keep the night waking going.
If too little daytime activity is the cause, giving more usually helps.
A vet check for pain and illness, especially in older cats.
Play hard in the evening, then feed; give no attention for night-time demands.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 1150 to 1156.
Ignoring briefly and then giving in teaches the cat to try harder.
Most cases improve within weeks to months when everyone is consistent.
Meet daily needs for play, company and a good diet, on a predictable schedule.
Give attention when the cat is calm, and nothing for pestering.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 1101 to 1116.
Kittens must be shown what is theirs to chew.
String, cords and hair ties are dangerous if swallowed.
The cat is not being spiteful; punishing it after the fact does not teach it anything.
Cover electrical cords and put small, stringy things away.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 1117 to 1124 and 1182 to 1188.
Some hybrid breeds, such as Bengals and Savannahs, may be more predatory.
Not all species can live safely together; small pets need protecting from cats.
Rigorous management: keep cats and small pets apart, and give cats daily hunting-style play.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 1157 to 1164.
Roaming intact cats produce unwanted kittens and spread parasites and disease.
Roaming cats are at greater risk of injury.
Containment and a richer home life resolve most cases.
Sterilise, enrich the home territory, and secure doors and windows.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 1165 to 1172.
Sudden movements, sharp turns, not being able to see out, and a full stomach make motion sickness worse.
A secure travel box keeps both the cat and the driver safe.
Scolding a frightened cat in the car makes it worse.
Leave the travel box out at home as a bed, with treats inside, so it means safety.
Drive smoothly; practise short trips that end well.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 1189 to 1196.
Cats outside the home and many cats in the area can set off crying.
Most problems need several weeks of steady work, and the cause has to be found.
Meet daily needs on a predictable schedule; reward quiet, not crying.
Where to check. Pike and Horwitz (2026), pp. 1197 to 1209.

passages.h: Repetitive habits, eating odd things, and old age
passages.x: Spinning, chasing lights, licking, sucking fabric, eating what is not food, and the changes of the senior years.
Stress, conflict, frustration, a dull environment and an unpredictable relationship with people all feed these habits; some breeds and family lines are prone.
Shouting at the dog can be heard as attention and keep the habit going.
Injuries to the tail mean the habit has become self-injurious and needs a vet.

People For Animals is India's largest animal welfare organisation, working through a nationwide network of independently registered Units: rescue, shelter and adoption, animal birth control and anti-rabies programmes, cruelty complaints and prosecution, enforcement of animal protection laws, and engagement with government on policy.

The Zonal Head is PFA's designated coordinator for all recognised and proposed Units within the assigned Zone. It is a field-based, enforcement- and movement-building role: growing PFA's presence across the Zone, building and mentoring local leadership and volunteers, ensuring an effective animal welfare and enforcement response on the ground, and coordinating with police, veterinary and civic authorities. Each Unit remains independently registered and self-governing; the Zonal Head coordinates and supports them and carries directions from the Principal Organisation.

Prompt, documented action on cruelty, abandonment, injury and neglect complaints:
Guide Units in registering complaints and FIRs and in invoking the strongest available provisions.
Secure custody of rescued or seized animals as case property under the PCA (Care and Maintenance of Case Property Animals) Rules, 2017, and ensure their care pending trial.

Maintain evidentiary discipline: dated photographs and video, witness details, veterinary certificates and a clear chain of custody, so cases survive prosecution rather than collapsing at the complaint stage.
Liaise with SHOs, prosecutors, veterinary officers and Honorary Animal Welfare Officers to see cases through to chargesheet and conviction, and track outcomes.

Companion and street animals : cruelty to dogs and cats including poisoning and illegal killing, feeding disputes with RWAs and authorities, unlawful relocation of community animals, gaps in ABC programmes.
Cattle and large animals : abandoned cattle, gaushala conditions, illegal and cruel transport, unlicensed and cruel slaughter, disease-driven distress.
Working animals : equines at brick kilns, tourism sites, weddings and construction; bullocks and draught animals; camels; unfit-to-work animals; lack of water, shade or farriery.
Farmed animals : battery cages, live-bird markets, piggeries, cruel handling in transport and markets.
Aquatic animals : live fish and seafood transport and market handling; the ornamental fish trade.

Wildlife and trade : poaching, snaring and trapping, illegal bird and exotic-pet trade (including CITES-listed species), monkey and parakeet capture, and rescues where people and wildlife share space.
Captive and performing animals : captive elephants and temple animals, circuses and unregistered performing animals, roadside menageries, animal-drawn-vehicle abuse.
Blood sports and rituals : cockfighting, dog and other animal fighting, bull-taming events, bullock-cart racing, cruelty in religious sacrifice.
Seasonal hazards : glass-coated kite string (manja) injuries to birds, festival firecracker distress, heat-wave, cold-wave and monsoon response.
Establishments : pet shops (Pet Shop Rules, 2018), dog breeders (Dog Breeding and Marketing Rules, 2017), livestock markets: registration, inspection and closure of illegal operators.
Trauma and access to care : road-accident and roadkill response, and access to first aid, ambulances and veterinary treatment.

passages.h: A festival of light. Not of fear.
passages.x: Every cracker is louder to a dog, a cat, a bird or a cow than it is to us, and they cannot know it will stop. Here is how to keep the animals around you safe, what Indian law allows, and how to celebrate without the noise.
Every ten decibels is ten times the sound. The bang of a single cracker at the legal limit carries ten thousand times the sound of heavy traffic.
The limit is 125 dB(AI), or 145 dB(C) at the peak, measured 4 metres from where the cracker bursts. A cracker louder than that may not be made, sold or burst in India.
When the Maharashtra Pollution Control Board tested 89 cracker brands in 2013, 30 broke the limit. The loudest single cracker reached 132.4 dB(A), and one bomb peaked at 152 dB(C).
Not only the dog on your sofa. Every animal within a few streets hears every cracker.
01 Dogs and cats at home. Many hide, shake, pant, stop eating or try to escape: through a window, off a balcony, out of a gate left open.
02 Dogs and cats on the street. They have no door to shut. They run onto roads and into other dogs' streets, and many are never seen again. Some have crackers thrown at them, or tied to them.
03 Birds. Crackers go off when birds are roosting. They take off in the dark, fly into wires and walls, and leave their nests and chicks behind.
04 Cows, horses and donkeys. Tied up, they cannot get away, and they hurt themselves pulling. A horse in a baraat stands beside the crackers and the band; a frightened horse bolts into the crowd.
05 Animals in the wild. Near forests, lakes and sanctuaries, the noise and the smoke drive animals away from where they feed and breed.
A little planning before the festival spares an animal a night of terror.
Walk your dog early, before the first crackers, and keep the lead on.
Put a collar with your phone number on every dog and cat.
Make a den in the quietest room: bedding, curtains drawn, a fan or the TV on.
If your animal panics every year, see your vet now. Never give a human medicine.
Stay home with them if you can. Speak calmly and carry on as normal.
Let them hide. Do not pull them out or scold them.
Watch the door: guests and deliveries are when animals bolt.
Keep cats in. Keep dogs off terraces and balconies.
Sweep up spent crackers, wire and paper. Dogs and cows eat them.
Look under cars, in drains and stairwells for animals hiding or hurt.
A burn: cool running water for ten to twenty minutes, then a vet. First aid for burns
Lost? Tell your neighbours, local groups and your nearest PFA unit at once.

Crackers go off across the year in India. Plan the same way every time.
Crackers are allowed in India only at set hours, only up to a set loudness, and never at an animal.
01 No crackers from 10 pm to 6 am. And none at any hour in a silence zone: 100 metres around a hospital, a school, a court or a place of worship. Supreme Court, In re Noise Pollution, 2005.

02 Two hours on a festival night. On Diwali and Gurpurab, crackers only between 8 and 10 pm, or the two hours your state sets. On Christmas Eve and New Year's Eve, 11:55 pm to 12:30 am. No series crackers (laris). In Delhi-NCR, only green crackers, and only on the days the Court allows. Supreme Court, Arjun Gopal v Union of India, 2018.
03 No cracker louder than 125 dB at 4 metres. A louder one may not be made, sold or burst. Environment (Protection) Rules, 1986.

04 Hurting an animal with a cracker is a crime. Throwing a cracker at an animal, or tying one to it, is cruelty under Section 11(1)(a) of the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960. Where it maims or kills, Section 325 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita carries up to five years, and the police must register an FIR.
An animal being hurt right now? Call 112 first.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.x: Before you cite any of this. Every answer names the provision it rests on, so you can check it rather than take it on trust. Read the section on indiacode.nic.in before you quote it, and check your State: prevention of cruelty is a concurrent subject, so State rules and municipal by-laws sit on top of everything here. A section cited wrongly in an FIR is harder to correct than one left out. Last read against the statutes in August 2026.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A1 Which law protects dogs from cruelty?
passages.x: Section 3 of the PCA Act 1960 puts a positive duty on anyone in charge of an animal to prevent unnecessary pain, so inaction is itself actionable. Section 11(1) then lists the offences: beating, kicking, overloading, starving, confining, abandoning and more.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A2 Which section carries a real sentence for cruelty?
passages.x: Where the animal is killed, poisoned, maimed or rendered useless, BNS Section 325 carries up to five years and is a cognizable offence, so the police are obliged to register an FIR rather than take a complaint and sit on it. It applies to any animal, owned or not, and the old value thresholds in IPC 428 and 429 are gone. Charge it there. The PCA Act alone is not worth filing under: its penalty has never been raised from the 1960 figures, and the 2022 amendment that would raise it is still not enacted.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A2 Which section carries a real sentence for cruelty?
passages.x: Careful Section 325 is mischief, so it needs an intentional act: starving, neglect and failure to treat are not mischief, and belong under PCA Section 11 read with Section 3. And it is bailable, so expect the accused to be released; the value of the section is that it forces registration and carries a real sentence at trial, not that it holds anyone.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A3 Is killing or maiming a dog a crime?
passages.x: BNS Section 325, which replaced IPC 428 and 429, punishes killing, poisoning, maiming or rendering useless any animal with up to five years, or fine, or both.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A3 Is killing or maiming a dog a crime?
passages.x: Do this Insist the FIR names Section 325 and not merely the PCA Act.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A4 Can one be jailed for poisoning community dogs?
passages.x: Section 11(1)(l) of the PCA Act protects street dogs by name from being poisoned with strychnine or harmed by any other unnecessarily cruel method. Add BNS Section 325 for the custodial sentence. Ask for a post mortem, because the toxicology report is the evidence the case rests on.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A5 What are the ABC Rules 2023?
passages.x: Rules framed under Section 38 of the PCA Act for managing community dogs: humane capture, sterilisation and vaccination, then return of the dog to the exact place it came from. Return to its own locality is the rule, not a concession. The local body must run the programme through an AWBI recognised organisation.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A6 Who is responsible for community dogs in my area?
passages.x: The local body, meaning your municipal corporation, city municipal council or gram panchayat.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A6 Who is responsible for community dogs in my area?
passages.x: The ABC Rules 2023 place the duty to run sterilisation and anti rabies vaccination on it, not on residents or feeders. If it has no ABC programme, that is a default you can act on in writing.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A7 Can community dogs be relocated?
passages.x: The ABC Rules require a sterilised and vaccinated dog to go back to its own locality, and relocation is not a lawful method of managing community dogs. The Supreme Court order of 19 May 2026 made a narrow exception for premises such as schools, hospitals, sports complexes, bus stands and railway stations: dogs from there are sterilised, vaccinated and given safe placement in a designated shelter, where they are to be cared for.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A7 Can community dogs be relocated?
passages.x: Do this Read that as a narrow exception, not a licence, and ask that any dog placed in a shelter receives proper care there.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A7 Can community dogs be relocated?
passages.x: Careful This is a continuing suo motu matter now monitored by every High Court, so check the current position before relying on it.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A8 What did the Supreme Court's May 2026 judgment say?
passages.x: That the ABC Rules remain the framework for humane management of community dogs, through sterilisation and vaccination; that dogs from schools, hospitals and similar premises are to be sterilised, vaccinated and given safe placement in a designated shelter; that every district must have at least one working ABC centre; and that officials who do not follow the directions are answerable. It also upheld the AWBI’s standard operating procedure, which is the document a municipality works from. The mandatory district centre is the part most useful to citizens and to the animals.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A8 What did the Supreme Court's May 2026 judgment say?
passages.x: Careful The proceedings continue and High Courts are monitoring compliance, so directions can move.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A9 When may a community dog be humanely euthanised?
passages.x: Only on three grounds under the 2026 directions, each to be assessed by qualified veterinary experts: rabies, an incurable illness causing suffering, or severe aggression established on evidence. A resident complaint is not a ground. It must be done humanely by a registered veterinarian. Anything else is an offence under BNS Section 325.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A9 When may a community dog be humanely euthanised?
passages.x: Careful The judgment says “rabid”, not “laboratory confirmed”, and the safeguard it names is assessment by qualified veterinary experts. Ask for that assessment on record rather than for a lab report the order does not require.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A10 Is feeding community dogs legal?
passages.x: Yes, and obstructing a feeder is the actionable conduct, not the feeding.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A10 Is feeding community dogs legal?
passages.x: The ABC Rules 2023 require resident associations and local bodies to designate feeding spots. The Delhi High Court in Dr Maya D. Chablani v. Radha Mittal (2021) held that community dogs have a right to food and that citizens have a right to feed them, subject to using designated points and keeping them clean.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A11 Can my apartment RWA ban pets or the feeding of community animals?
passages.x: A resident association is a private body and cannot override rules made under a central Act. AWBI guidelines and repeated High Court rulings hold that an RWA cannot ban pets, bar them from lifts, or prohibit feeding. It may regulate reasonably, meaning time and place, and nothing more.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A11 Can my apartment RWA ban pets or the feeding of community animals?
passages.x: Careful The May 2026 judgment read “gated campus” in the ABC Rules narrowly, so a society enclosing a school, hospital or similar premises may stand differently from an ordinary residential block.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A12 Can a housing society fine me for my dog barking?
passages.x: Barking is not a ground for sending the animal away, and AWBI guidance says so directly. A resolution passed by a majority does not become lawful merely because it was passed.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A13 Do I need a dog licence?
passages.x: It depends on your local body, since this is a municipal by-law subject and not a central one.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A13 Do I need a dog licence?
passages.x: Many corporations require annual registration of pet dogs. Check Udupi City Municipal Council for the local position. Registration is also the quickest way to bring your dog home if it is ever lost or taken in by the municipality.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.x: Rabies is notifiable under the PCICDA 2009, and annual anti rabies vaccination is required for municipal registration, for travel, and for the National Action Plan for Dog Mediated Rabies Elimination by 2030.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A15 Are Pitbulls and Rottweilers banned in India?
passages.x: A central letter of March 2024 asked States to prohibit 23 breeds. Within weeks six High Courts had set it aside or stayed it, two quashing it outright, for want of consultation with the people it affected and for treating breed as a proxy for danger.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A15 Are Pitbulls and Rottweilers banned in India?
passages.x: Do this Check your own municipality, but a mere advisory is not law.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A16 Do dog breeders need a licence?
passages.x: The Dog Breeding and Marketing Rules 2017 require registration with the State Animal Welfare Board, minimum housing and veterinary standards, and record keeping. A female may not be bred below 18 months or more than once a year. An unregistered breeder is operating illegally, and photographs of the premises are worth more than a complaint.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A17 Do pet shops need a licence?
passages.x: The Pet Shop Rules 2018 require registration with the State Animal Welfare Board, space and veterinary norms, and prohibit the sale of animals under eight weeks old. Selling from an unregistered shop is an offence under the parent PCA Act.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A18 Can one buy a puppy online or on the roadside?
passages.x: Sale by an unregistered breeder or seller violates the 2017 and 2018 Rules.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A18 Can one buy a puppy online or on the roadside?
passages.x: The buyer is not usually prosecuted, but has almost no remedy when the animal turns out to be sick or underage, and buying sustains the trade the Rules exist to stop. The useful step is the other way round: report the seller to the State Animal Welfare Board, which is the authority those Rules make responsible for registration, with the listing, the address and any photographs. Where animals are kept in conditions that cause suffering, that is also Section 11 of the PCA Act.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A19 Is ear cropping or tail docking legal?
passages.x: Section 11(1)(l) of the PCA Act prohibits mutilating an animal, and cosmetic cropping or docking has no medical justification. The AWBI circular of 2011 and Veterinary Council ethics treat it as professional misconduct, so the veterinarian who performs it can be proceeded against.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.x: Section 11(1)(m) covers organising, keeping or using premises for animal fighting, and Section 11(1)(n) covers promoting a fight or merely being present at one. Spectators are liable. Where a dog dies, add BNS Section 325.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A21 Can one abandon a dog?
passages.x: Section 11(1)(i) makes it an offence to abandon an animal in circumstances likely to cause it suffering from starvation or thirst. If the animal dies, the abandonment becomes a killing and BNS Section 325 applies. Surrender to a shelter instead, which is lawful.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A22 Can one keep a dog chained all day?
passages.x: Section 11(1)(f) specifically prohibits keeping an animal chained on an unreasonably short or heavy chain for an unreasonable period.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A22 Can one keep a dog chained all day?
passages.x: Do this Read with the Section 3 duty of care, prolonged tethering is cruelty on its face and photographs establish it.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A23 What are the rules for transporting dogs?
passages.x: The Transport of Animals Rules 1978 prescribe crate size, ventilation, water and a veterinary fitness certificate for rail and air. Independently, Section 11(1)(d) of the PCA Act makes conveying an animal in a way that causes unnecessary pain an offence, so a breach of the Rules and a cruelty offence usually arise on the same facts.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A24 Can I take my dog on a train?
passages.x: Indian Railways permits dogs in a first class AC coupe or first class cabin on booking, or in the brake van dog box. Carry the vaccination certificate. Confining an animal in the brake van without water or ventilation remains cruelty regardless of the ticket.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A25 Can I fly with my dog in India?
passages.x: Yes, in cabin or cargo depending on the airline, with health and vaccination certificates.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A25 Can I fly with my dog in India?
passages.x: Each carrier sets its own crate and weight conditions under DGCA guidance. The Transport of Animals Rules still govern the crate itself.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A26 How do I bring a dog into India from abroad?
passages.x: You need a no objection certificate from the Animal Quarantine and Certification Service, a microchip, a rabies antibody titre and a health certificate, within the DGFT import conditions. Pets brought as baggage on transfer of residence are permitted subject to those conditions.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A27 Who is responsible for compensation after a dog bite?
passages.x: Courts in Kerala and the Punjab and Haryana High Court have awarded compensation against local bodies for failing to run ABC programmes, and the Supreme Court in 2026 discussed fixing liability on defaulting local bodies. The claim lies against the authority that neglected its ABC duty.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A28 What if my pet dog bites someone?
passages.x: You face civil liability and possible prosecution for negligent conduct with an animal under BNS Section 291, which replaced IPC Section 289. Keep the animal leashed in public and keep vaccination proof. A current anti rabies certificate is the single most useful document you can hold.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A29 Is a leash compulsory in public?
passages.x: Under most municipal by-laws, yes, and some require muzzling for larger dogs.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A29 Is a leash compulsory in public?
passages.x: This is a by-law question, so the answer is set by your corporation and not by the PCA Act. Non compliance also weakens your position if a bite is alleged.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A30 Can community dogs be sterilised privately, or only through the ABC programme?
passages.x: Under the ABC Rules 2023, humane capture, surgery and return must be done by an AWBI recognised organisation, with trained handlers and registered veterinarians at a recognised facility. This protects the dog: unauthorised capture is a breach of the Rules and, if it causes pain, an offence under Section 11.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A31 Can police or the municipality pick up my pet dog?
passages.x: Not a collared, registered pet, which must be returned to you.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A31 Can police or the municipality pick up my pet dog?
passages.x: A municipality may take in an animal only within its by-laws, for example one that is unowned and unclaimed, or where a veterinary or court process requires it, and the animal’s welfare must be protected throughout.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A31 Can police or the municipality pick up my pet dog?
passages.x: Do this Keep the registration and tag on the dog, because identification is what converts this from a dispute into a simple return.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.x: The Animal Welfare Board of India, a statutory body constituted under Section 4 of the PCA Act.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.x: It advises the central government, issues guidelines and advisories, recognises ABC organisations, and appoints Honorary Animal Welfare Officers who can assist at the scene.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A33 Can I report cruelty, and to whom?
passages.x: Go to the police and insist on an FIR under BNS Section 325 read with Section 11 of the PCA Act. Section 325 is cognizable, and Section 173 of the BNSS 2023, which replaced Section 154 of the CrPC, obliges the officer to register information disclosing a cognizable offence. Say both things at the counter: the section, and that it is cognizable. If refused, write to the Superintendent of Police and then move the Magistrate under Section 175(3).

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A34 Is it illegal to leave a dog in a parked car?
passages.x: Confining an animal in a space that does not allow it a reasonable opportunity for movement, or keeping it in conditions causing unnecessary suffering, falls under Section 11(1)(e) and Section 11(1)(g). In summer this is also a killing risk, which brings in BNS Section 325.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A35 Are dogs allowed in parks?
passages.x: Public parks may restrict access by by-law.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A35 Are dogs allowed in parks?
passages.x: A resident society cannot impose a blanket ban on pets using common areas, per AWBI guidance. The distinction matters: a municipal by-law is law, a society circular is not.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A36 Can a landlord refuse tenants with dogs?
passages.x: A landlord can set lease terms before you sign, and that is a contract question.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A36 Can a landlord refuse tenants with dogs?
passages.x: Once you are in occupation, the society cannot force you to give up the animal, since that is governed by AWBI guidance and the case law on pets in housing.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A37 Are there rules on dog kennels and boarding?
passages.x: Boarding and kennelling are treated in several states under the pet shop and breeding registration framework, and AWBI guidance applies to housing, space and veterinary cover. The PCA duty of care in Section 3 applies to the boarder for the whole period the animal is in their charge.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A38 What is the national rabies programme?
passages.x: The National Rabies Control Programme, together with the National Action Plan for Dog Mediated Rabies Elimination by 2030, which pairs mass dog vaccination with free anti rabies vaccine for bite victims at government hospitals. Vaccinating dogs and protecting people with free vaccine, not displacing dogs, is the strategy the state has committed to.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A39 Is it legal to shoot a dog on a farm?
passages.x: Killing an animal attracts BNS Section 325 and Section 11 of the PCA Act. Private defence is a narrow exception that requires a real and immediate threat to life, and it is judged after the fact on the facts. Property protection is not a defence.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A40 Can dogs be used in films and advertisements?
passages.x: Section 22 of the PCA Act restricts exhibition and training of performing animals, and the Performing Animals (Registration) Rules 2001 require registration with the AWBI and a pre shoot no objection certificate. Shooting without it is an offence and the footage is evidence of it.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A41 Is street dog community ownership recognised?
passages.x: The ABC Rules 2023 recognise community animals and the role of caregivers, and give feeders both standing and duties: use the designated spot, keep it clean, and cooperate with sterilisation drives. That recognition is what a feeder cites when an association objects.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A42 Can a municipality label a dog aggressive?
passages.x: Only through the committee process in the ABC Rules, on evidence.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A42 Can a municipality label a dog aggressive?
passages.x: The 2026 directions require evidence, assessed by qualified veterinary experts, rather than the volume of complaints, and a dog is entitled to humane treatment throughout.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A42 Can a municipality label a dog aggressive?
passages.x: Do this Ask to see the committee's finding, since a label applied without one is open to challenge.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A43 What if the local body is not doing ABC?
passages.x: Complain in writing to the Municipal Commissioner and the District Collector, and keep the acknowledgement.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A43 What if the local body is not doing ABC?
passages.x: The Supreme Court in 2026 required Chief Secretaries to report district ABC centres to the High Courts, so the default is already on record. Beyond that, a writ petition under Article 226 lies against the authority.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A44 Can I run a private dog shelter?
passages.x: Register as a society or trust, and seek AWBI recognition, which is needed for ABC work and helps with grants. Shelter conditions themselves are governed by the Section 3 duty of care, so overcrowding in a shelter is as much an offence as it is anywhere else.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A45 Is dog meat legal in India?
passages.x: Dogs are not a food animal under the Food Safety and Standards framework, so slaughter and sale for meat has no licence route and is unlawful. Transport for that purpose also attracts the PCA Act and BNS Section 325.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A46 Are guard dog owners liable for injuries to trespassers?
passages.x: Courts expect visible warning and effective control, and negligent keeping attracts BNS Section 291, the successor to IPC Section 289. Signage and secure fencing are the practical defence.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A47 Should I get my dog microchipped?
passages.x: It is voluntary in most places, mandatory for import and export, and required by some municipal registration schemes.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A47 Should I get my dog microchipped?
passages.x: It is also the most reliable proof of ownership if your dog is picked up or stolen.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A48 What can be done when dogs are overloaded in crates or vehicles?
passages.x: Section 11(1)(a) covers overloading and Section 11(1)(d) covers conveyance causing unnecessary pain, alongside the Transport of Animals Rules 1978. The vehicle can be stopped and the animals seized, and the animals can be placed in custody pending trial rather than returned to the accused.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A49 Are electric or prong collars banned?
passages.x: There is no specific prohibition by name.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A49 Are electric or prong collars banned?
passages.x: Use that causes pain or injury is prosecutable under Section 11(1)(a) read with the Section 3 duty of care, and a veterinary report describing the injury is what carries such a complaint.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: A50 Where do I find the official texts?
passages.x: The bare Acts and Rules are on indiacode.nic.in, the ABC Rules 2023 and AWBI guidelines are on awbi.gov.in, and reported judgments are on the Supreme Court and High Court websites. Quote the section, not a summary, whenever it matters.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: B1 Which law governs cattle slaughter?
passages.x: Your State's cattle preservation Act, not the PCA Act.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: B1 Which law governs cattle slaughter?
passages.x: Cattle slaughter is a State subject, so each State has its own Act naming which animals are protected, what age or fitness certificate is needed, and the punishment. Most such Acts carry imprisonment measured in years, far heavier than the PCA Act. Look up your State's Act on indiacode.nic.in and cite its section, because the PCA Act on its own will not carry a slaughter case.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: B2 Is cow slaughter banned across India?
passages.x: It is a State subject under Entry 15 of the State List, so the position differs by State. Most northern and western States impose near total bans; Kerala, West Bengal and most of the North East do not; several fall between, protecting cows but not buffalo or bulls. Article 48 of the Constitution directs States towards prohibition, but it is a directive principle and not directly enforceable.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.x: Some Acts protect buffalo outright, some only below a stated age, and some not at all. Where an age or fitness condition applies, the Act usually requires a certificate from a named authority before slaughter, and slaughter without that certificate is the offence. Several State Acts also put the burden of proving that a slaughter was lawful on the accused.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.x: Do this Read your State's Act for the animal list and the certificate rule before you complain.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: B4 What is the punishment under a State cattle Act?
passages.x: It varies by State, but the pattern is the same: imprisonment measured in years, fines in lakhs, more for a repeat offence, and power to seize the animals and the vehicle used. That is the provision to cite in a cattle transport case, not the PCA Act, whose penalties are small. Find the punishment section of your State's Act and quote it in the complaint.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: B5 Who can seize cattle being transported illegally?
passages.x: A police officer not below the rank prescribed in the Act, or an authorised officer, may seize the cattle and the vehicle. Ask that the seizure memo record the number of animals, their condition and the vehicle registration, because that document decides what happens to the animals afterwards.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: B6 Where do seized cattle go?
passages.x: The Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (Care and Maintenance of Case Property Animals) Rules 2017 allow a Magistrate to give custody of animals seized as case property to an animal welfare organisation pending trial, rather than returning them to the accused. This is the single most useful rule in a live seizure.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: B7 Can seized cattle be returned to the accused?
passages.x: Under the Case Property Animals Rules 2017 the court may entrust the animals to an infirmary or welfare organisation, and returning them to a person facing a cruelty or slaughter charge defeats the purpose of the seizure.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: B7 Can seized cattle be returned to the accused?
passages.x: Do this File an application citing those Rules as soon as the seizure is made.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: B8 How many cattle may be carried in a truck?
passages.x: The Transport of Animals Rules 1978 set the numbers by vehicle size, and overcrowding is the norm in illegal transport.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: B8 How many cattle may be carried in a truck?
passages.x: Overloading is an offence under Section 11(1)(a) and conveyance causing unnecessary pain under Section 11(1)(d). Count the animals and photograph the deck; the count is the offence.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: B9 Is tying cattle legs during transport an offence?
passages.x: Binding legs, roping animals together, or packing them so they cannot stand causes unnecessary pain and falls squarely within Section 11(1)(d) read with the Transport of Animals Rules 1978. It is also the clearest visual evidence available at a checkpost.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: B10 What permits are needed to transport cattle between States?
passages.x: A valid transport permit, a veterinary certificate of fitness for the journey, and compliance with the Transport of Animals Rules 1978. Where the State has a cattle preservation Act, movement for slaughter is separately restricted by it, and many States require a permit for taking cattle out of the State at all. Absence of a fitness certificate is itself a violation you can point to on the spot.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: B11 Is cattle smuggling across the border an offence?
passages.x: Yes, and the Supreme Court in the Gauri Maulekhi litigation directed States to prevent illegal transport of cattle across the border to Nepal for sacrifice. Add the Customs Act and the State cattle preservation law to the PCA charges.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: B12 Can a gaushala be prosecuted for neglect?
passages.x: Section 3 places the duty of care on whoever has charge of the animal, and a gaushala has charge. Starvation, denial of water, or leaving carcasses among living animals attracts Section 11(1)(h) and Section 11(1)(j). Registration as a charity is not a shield.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: B13 What is phooka or doom dev?
passages.x: Injecting air or any substance into a cow to make it yield more milk.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: B13 What is phooka or doom dev?
passages.x: Section 12 of the PCA Act creates a separate offence for it, punishable with fine and imprisonment, and the animal can be forfeited to the government. It is one of the few PCA sections with a forfeiture consequence worth invoking.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: B14 Is oxytocin use on dairy cattle legal?
passages.x: Oxytocin for milk letdown is prohibited, its sale is restricted under the Drugs and Cosmetics framework, and administering an injurious drug to an animal is an offence under Section 12 and Section 11(1)(c) of the PCA Act. Seize the vial, since possession on a dairy is the evidence.

passages.t: Animal law in India: cruelty, dog bites, FIRs
passages.h: B15 Can calves be separated from cows immediately after birth?
passages.x: There is no provision that prohibits separation by name.
